30919b3025af.t: A Fine Hour in That Month of July

c3a89844d3c5.t: End where the Traditions began. Bill W. wrote (A.A. Comes of Age): "In the summer of 1950 we held our first international convention in Cleveland, Ohio. About 3,000 were in attendance." Dr. Bob was dying and everyone knew it — five of the previous seven months in bed — and he stood up anyway, and chose the smallest words he had (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers): "Our Twelve Steps, when simmered down to the last, resolve themselves into the words 'love' and 'service.' We understand what love is, and we understand what service is. So let's bear those two things in mind." Then the Convention did what this whole year of readings has been about — Bill called it (A.A. Comes of Age) "the confirmation of our Twelve Traditions by the Convention as the permanent platform of unity and function". A recording preserves "the Convention's unanimous voice of consent." His verdict: "It was a fine hour in that month of July, 1950." Three hundred sixty-six readings end here, on purpose: a dying founder asking for simplicity, and a room of anonymous alcoholics answering with one voice that principles would govern from now on. You can still listen to the yes.

6a03bef319ec.t: December 4 — "The Thursday Meeting Had a Star." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. He is eleven years sober, funny in the wa

2833987d0e82.t: The Thursday Meeting Had a Star

1f4969d29d24.t: He is eleven years sober, funny in the way that keeps a room warm. Nobody decides anything — it accumulates. Visitors ask whether he's on this week. The group, sensibly, schedules him: first Thursday of the month. On his Thursdays, sixty chairs; other weeks, twenty-five. It runs three years and helps a great many people — which is the difficulty, because in March his firm moves him two provinces away, and by June the Thursday meeting votes to fold itself into Tuesday's. No one did anything wrong. He never asked for the crowd and often looked uneasy in it. The meeting had simply stopped being a group with a speaker and become an audience with a habit, and an audience goes where the show goes. A group organized around a principle can lose any member and hold. A group organized around a person is one job transfer from the end.

1e91c875193e.t: The meeting was an audience before anyone noticed, and it closed when its star moved away. Which room am I in for the principle, and which for a person?

b25fe47181cf.t: December 5 — "Renamed as Shame." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. The argument arrives sounding like liberation: anonymity

bc1d6114f192.t: The argument arrives sounding like liberation: anonymity is stigma in a virtue's clothes, and people should recover out loud. The mechanism is renaming — take a spiritual discipline, call it a symptom, and every act of humility reads as evidence of the disease. Once the frame sets, publicity becomes the prescription and the Tradition becomes the problem. But the definition was written first (A.A. pamphlet P-43): "Anonymity, as we observe it in A.A., is at root a simple expression of humility." And the program's stated aim runs dead against the shame reading: "to put our self-respect on a solid base of truth, rather than on fantasies about ourselves." A member practicing this Tradition is not hiding in disgrace. He is declining to be enlarged. Different acts, different engines — and only one of them has anything to do with shame.

7c910c57231a.t: The capture renames humility as a symptom, so publicity can be prescribed as the cure. Where have I let someone rename a thing I do — and then treated the new name as true?

b2ce692d9930.t: December 6 — "The Stark Fact." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. Around 1949 Bill put it to Dr. Bob in writing, unsoftened

a0cb24e7e9f8.t: Around 1949 Bill put it to Dr. Bob in writing, unsoftened (Pass It On): "The stark fact is that you and I still head Alcoholics Anonymous. By common consent, we remain the only two individuals in A.A. actually entitled and expected to speak for the whole." Fifteen years in, the fellowship of no names had two heads. The cost ran both ways. Bill's psychiatrist had a thesis about it, and Bill repeated it with approval: "So we have the person of Mr. Anonymous in conflict with Bill Wilson." The shelter every other drunk enjoyed was closed to its architects: "Wherever he went, he was sooner or later spotted, named, and asked to lead." Dr. Bob's first reply was doubt — "Maybe I am wrong, but that is the way I feel. Love, Smithy." The founders were the Tradition's last exception, and both men had begun to see that the exception was the threat.

0070ffa46820.t: The fellowship of no names still had two, and the two knew it was unsound. What am I the standing exception to — and who consented to that?

abface542cbf.t: Grounded in: Pass It On (Bill's letter to Dr. Bob; "Mr. Anonymous").

d1a7e3c86b5c.t: December 7 — "The Back of His Head." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. A.A.'s biography of Bill records the offer (Pass It

245412244853.t: A.A.'s biography of Bill records the offer (Pass It On): "When Time magazine wanted to put Bill on its cover — that is, put the back of his head on the front of the magazine — Bill declined, and declined the cover story as well." Read the offer again: it already conceded his anonymity. No face, no name, technically inside the letter of the Tradition. He refused anyway, and his accounting is the hardest arithmetic in A.A.'s history: "I denied recovery to an awful lot of alcoholics — some of these may already be dead." What he weighed against those lives was what the piece would manufacture: "a clear and colorful public image of me as a person." One image, then a precedent, then every power-driver holding a clipping that proves it's allowed. "Therefore, I declined the publicity, and I must confess it wasn't easy." The Tradition was not kept by men who found it painless. It was kept by a man who counted the cost and paid it.

6ad4757e60f5.t: The offer already protected his anonymity, and he refused it for what it would build. What have I kept technically inside the rules while constructing what the rules exist to prevent?

3ce698cd1199.t: Grounded in: Pass It On (the Time cover offer).

a392cd08705f.t: December 8 — "Faceless Automatons." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. This Tradition has a failure mode, and Bill named it.

05afa71ac95b.t: This Tradition has a failure mode, and Bill named it. Writing on leadership in 1959 (A.A. Service Manual), he watched the phrase become a muzzle: "We are apt to warp the traditional idea of “principles before personalities” around to such a point that there would be no “personality” in leadership whatever. This would imply rather faceless automatons trying to please everybody, regardless." You have seen the warp: the capable member who won't stand for a position because standing looks like ego; the strong proposal withdrawn at the first frown; a group mistaking the absence of initiative for the presence of humility. That is the Tradition inverted — ego managed by hiding instead of by service. Bill's corrective sits in the same essay: "Our leaders do not drive by mandate, they lead by example." Personalities are not the enemy; personalities enthroned are.

ddae86b9a132.t: Bill himself warned that this Tradition can be warped into a demand for facelessness. Where am I calling it humility when it is actually hiding?

87dc7bdd9574.t: Grounded in: A.A. Service Manual (Bill W., "Leadership in A.A.: Ever a Vital Need," 1959).

60845d0ea900.t: Nine Years in the Same Chair

736916f13a92.t: He started the meeting nine years ago — found the church basement, paid the first month's rent himself, carried the literature box in his trunk. He hasn't held a position in six years, which is the elegant part: he doesn't need one. New secretaries check with him before changing the format. The treasurer asks him, not the group, about the rent. The group conscience votes with his eyebrows. Then in February he lands in hospital for six weeks, and the group discovers what it is: nobody else knows the landlord's number, which key opens the cupboard, or why the rent has stayed forty dollars under market. The meeting doesn't die. It finds out it was never quite a group — it was a man with attendees. To his credit, when he comes back he sits in the fourth row and lets them keep it. That is the day it becomes a group.

3311af94259e.t: For nine years the group conscience voted with one man's eyebrows, and it took his hospital bed to prove it. What runs only because I am standing next to it?

f2cfbc27c037.t: Twelve months. Twelve Traditions. October is Tradition 10.

d14ccd076d8b.t: A way out for half a million alcoholics died because it took sides in public fights, and the first thing it lost was the drunk. Bill W. told the story of the Washingtonians, a movement a century older than A.A. (A.A. Comes of Age): "At first the society was composed entirely of alcoholics trying to help one another." Their membership "passed the five hundred thousand mark." Then they "permitted politicians and reformers, both alcoholic and nonalcoholic, to use the society for their own purposes." Speakers took sides on slavery. Some became temperance crusaders, out to dry up the whole country. "Within a very few years they had completely lost their effectiveness in helping alcoholics, and the society collapsed." That is why the long form of Tradition 10 names "alcohol reform" by name (Big Book, p. 565). A drinker who hears that the rooms are for or against his party, his church or his bar has one more reason never to walk in. Today the pull comes as a campaign: a drinking law, a funding fight, and somebody speaking for "the recovery community" as if the people in the rooms had signed on. Test it tonight: ask whether your meeting's name appears anywhere outside the room, on anybody's side.

b3fb748fcc62.t: Half a million sober alcoholics lost their power to help the next drunk once their society took sides in public. Is there a drinker who would stay out of my room because of a side it has taken?

3ef28c10fd3c.t: <0>Short form: pp. 561–562. Long form: pp. 563–566.</0> If you only ever read one, read the long one.

595857dafcc4.t: The Twelve Traditions were adopted in 1950 for one reason: to stop A.A. from being <0>owned</0>. Not owned by a benefactor, not by a treatment centre, not by whoever happened to be paying the rent. They are the Fellowship's constitution — written out of near-misses A.A. actually lived through.

4ebe53edf3ef.t: Most of what circulates online quotes only the short form (pp. 561–562) and quietly drops the rest. So we front-load <0>the Long Form, pp. 563–566</0> — where the Traditions actually say what they mean. Tradition 3's clause that a group is A.A. only if "as a group, they have no other affiliation"? That exists <1>only</1> in the Long Form. It's the clause that says no treatment centre can own an A.A. group. It's also the clause the internet forgot.

6403ca028b80.t: One more thing, because it gets blurred constantly: <0>the Traditions are governance, not theology.</0> They bind A.A. groups and the Fellowship — not individuals. They are not a rulebook for your personal life.

0603f72e2225.t: <0>How August reads.</0> The month opens day-by-day — one angle on the Tradition at a time, where groups go wrong with it and the reason it was written — then settles into five questions, run straight through: <1>what specifically threatened A.A.</1> · <2>how the founders solved it before there was a Tradition</2> · <3>where that same danger lives now</3> · <4>how a group drifts off it on its own</4> · <5>how it gets hollowed out from outside</5>. Anything inside quotation marks is A.A.'s own wording, printed exactly, with the source named at the foot of the reading. The explaining around it is ours — plain modern English, and scenes drawn to show how the Tradition actually plays out. You should always be able to tell which is which.

382ec48763cb.t: Picture a group that says yes to a big outside gift — a bequest, no strings, everyone relieved. For a while the basket feels optional. Then the next gift arrives with a quiet expectation. Then a dispute over money nobody in the room earned. The Long Form doesn't soften it: accepting large gifts, or any contribution "carrying any obligation whatever, is unwise," and nothing "can so surely destroy our spiritual heritage as futile disputes over property, money, and authority." The danger was never the dollar. It's what the dollar asks for later.

5dfd438fde11.t: Flip the fundraiser and you find Tradition 7's quiet dignity: a Fellowship that pays its own way never has to perform for a donor. No banner to hang, no benefactor to please, no check that comes with a leash. There's a freedom in that most of us never knew while we were drinking — not needing anyone's money or approval to keep the door open. Self-support isn't A.A. being proud. 12dcf226cf53.t: November 1 — "The Credit." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. May 1940. The catcher for

7236d4f35e9c.t: May 1940. The catcher for the Cleveland Indians had just caught a no-hit game pitched by Bob Feller, and Rollie H. told the papers he had been sober in A.A. for a year. Before you decide what you think of him, take the reason. His drinking had been public knowledge, and when the story of his recovery broke, the credit went to the Oxford Group — he had stayed on with them after the Akron members left. Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers records what happened: "At that time, however, Rollie broke his silence and said no, the credit for his sobriety belonged to Alcoholics Anonymous." He did not do it for attention. He did it to correct a record that had A.A.'s work under somebody else's name. And it worked, exactly as he hoped. Bill W. wrote later (Pass It On) that "it did us plenty of good, temporarily, because alcoholics flocked in." Hundreds of them. It was also the first anonymity break the Fellowship had ever had at the national level, and A.A. has been arguing with itself about that week ever since.

93d3eabee01c.t: A man broke his anonymity to give A.A. credit it was being denied, hundreds of alcoholics came in because of it, and it was still the break that started everything. When has the generous thing I did spent something that wasn't mine to spend?

612f70e3ff00.t: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (Rollie H., May 1940); Pass It On.

7752d97347e5.t: November 10 — "Filmed Beside It." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. Nobody has to claim

38c09ec7a142.t: Nobody has to claim an endorsement to collect one. The mechanism is proximity, and it is almost impossible to object to. A film crew shoots outside the building where the meeting is held. A promotional video is recorded in the hall an hour before the chairs go out. A photograph is taken at the door, with the sign in shot. No word is spoken about A.A. and none needs to be — the viewer supplies the connection, which is the entire reason the location was chosen. What has happened is that an outside body has borrowed the visual credibility of a Fellowship that has no mechanism for lending it and no committee that could have refused. The long form's phrase (Big Book, p. 565) is "Our relations with the general public should be characterized by personal anonymity," and the difficulty here is that nothing personal was broken. A building was filmed. But the building is where the anonymity lives, and after that footage runs, everyone who walks in has been seen walking in.

7f7a83bcb06e.t: No one claimed anything and no name was given — a building was filmed, and afterwards everyone who walks in has been seen walking in. What have I been associated with purely by standing near it?

8c1f43fe093d.t: November 11 — "Carried Away With the Desire to Serve." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films

4965a00843f8.t: Carried Away With the Desire to Serve

b8f50bb058af.t: October 1939. There was no Tradition Eleven — there were no Traditions at all — and a man in Detroit who had never made a speech in his life got himself onto the radio. A.A.'s history of its co-founder sets down the date (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers): "In October 1939, Archie managed to get a six-minute radio interview about his recovery in A.A. It was heard in a number of Midwest cities and certainly represented a first for the area." His own account sits in the Big Book (p. 254), and the phrase he chose for himself years afterward is the one to keep. "I, carried away with the desire to serve A.A., gave what was probably one of the first radio broadcasts about A.A., living through a case of mike fright and feeling like a million dollars when it was all over." Carried away with the desire to serve. He is not confessing to vanity and there is no sign of any — he was frightened, he did it anyway, and it helped. But notice what he could not possibly have had: any way of knowing where that ends. Nobody had it yet. This Tradition exists because a great many people just like Archie were each, individually, right.

9ca26506a776.t: A frightened man got himself on the radio out of nothing but a desire to help, and there was no way yet for anyone to know where it led. What am I doing for good reasons whose cost nobody has worked out yet?

8af1660836eb.t: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (October 1939); Big Book p. 254 ("The Man Who Mastered Fear").

8402b59e14d3.t: November 12 — "There Was No Dr. Armstrong." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. On 1 Marc

d4065820677a.t: On 1 March 1941 the <0>Saturday Evening Post</0> ran Jack Alexander's article, and A.A. was never small again (Big Book, p. xviii) — "By March 1941 the membership had shot up to 2,000," and within the year it was four times that. Read the article and you meet a physician (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers) who is "still struggling to patch up his practice. The going is hard. He is in debt because of his contributions to the movement and the time he devotes gratis to alcoholics." The book calls him Dr. Armstrong. There was no Dr. Armstrong. It was Dr. Bob, printed under a false name to protect his own — the co-founder of A.A. appearing in the most important article ever written about it as somebody else entirely. Later, when a second Alexander piece was being prepared, Sister Ignatia asked Bill to keep her name out of that one. She was not a member; she was the nun who had admitted alcoholics to St. Thomas Hospital when nobody else would. Bill's answer drew the line exactly where the Tradition draws it. "To be anonymous, Sister, you'll have to take a little drink."

56b0bea57996.t: A.A.'s co-founder let himself be printed as a stranger so that the rule he asked others to keep would hold for him first. What would I give up to keep a rule I have asked other people to follow?

5bc7e457d8a5.t: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (the Post article; Sister Ignatia); Big Book p. xviii.

e86097c34c23.t: November 13 — "Not in the Meaning of This Tradition." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films.

f2543cc693d8.t: Not in the Meaning of This Tradition

9b6a30e316a6.t: This is the line the internet gets wrong more often than any other, and getting it wrong costs people at the margin. A.A.'s own literature, plainly (A.A. pamphlet P-43): "When people are asked what led them to seek A.A. help, the answer given most often is: "An A.A. member." Their chances would have been slim if all of us had remained completely in hiding. But many of us have chosen to tell our friends, neighbors, employers, co-workers, doctors, or spiritual advisers that we are in A.A. — and when we do so, we are not breaking our anonymity in the meaning of this Tradition." We are not breaking our anonymity. Telling your doctor is not a break. Telling your employer is not a break. Telling the man at work whose hands shake at nine in the morning is the single most effective thing anyone has ever done for this Fellowship, and it is precisely what the Tradition was built to keep possible. The level named is press, radio and films. Not the kitchen. Not the ward. Not the front seat of a car in a parking lot at four in the afternoon.

fd63d84d8e80.t: Telling one person face to face is not a break — it is what most members say brought them in. Who is the one person I could say it to quietly, with no camera anywhere near it?

32bdd80442ee.t: Grounded in: P-43 (Tradition Eleven); long form, Tradition 11.

6b4f62508c19.t: November 14 — "A Stranger on a Deadline." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. A reporter

efa09c368c89.t: A reporter rings the number on the intergroup site, because the paper is running something about the new detox unit and wants a line from A.A. The GSR takes it, since she is the one who answers that phone. She is careful. She says she can't speak for A.A. as a whole. She gives the meeting times, explains what the Fellowship does and does not do, and gives her name the way she gives it in the rooms — first name, last initial. The reporter is decent and barely interested in her. But a copy editor at ten at night has a house style, the paper does not print initials, and her surname is in the phone book. It runs on page five beneath the words Alcoholics Anonymous. She did everything right except the one thing nobody had told her: the decision about how her name appeared was never hers to make. A.A. put it as sharply as it can be put (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers) — an A.A. "who permits his name to appear in the press in connection with matters pertaining to A.A." has broken this Tradition. Permits. Nobody asked her.

0ec7b5385a42.t: She did everything right, and how her name appeared was decided by a stranger on a deadline. What am I trusting somebody else to get right on my behalf, without ever having agreed it?

1d6e0de615c5.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 11; Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (the A.A. Grapevine, February 1969).

92a8409b7ba8.t: November 15 — "Statistics Do Not Move Money." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. A chari

30e84542f2da.t: A charity that helps the same people A.A. helps has to raise money before the quarter closes, and the appeal needs one story. Statistics do not move money. A person does. So somebody who got well is asked for four paragraphs, and he writes them gladly, because the charity did help him and he wants it to survive. The appeal goes out with his photograph, his first name, and the sentence that makes the whole thing work: he found sobriety in Alcoholics Anonymous. Every word of it is true. Nobody has claimed A.A. supports the charity. But that letter now carries A.A.'s name as the guarantor of an outcome it is selling, inside a document whose only purpose is to produce a donation — and A.A.'s name is doing the part of the job the charity's own record could not do by itself. The Tradition warns against "sensational advertising," which sounds antique until you notice what advertising is: somebody else's message, with our credibility loaned to it, working.

193278908e06.t: Nobody lied and nobody claimed anything — one true sentence about where he got well did the work a charity's own record could not. What true thing about me has been used to carry an argument I never made?

010ba9c10580.t: November 16 — "On Celluloid." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. By the mid-1940s A.A. h

0f5eff1a3a6a.t: By the mid-1940s A.A. had become something it never planned to be — fashionable. A.A.'s own biography records it (Pass It On): "A.A. was by now a household word; it had gotten almost unanimously good reviews in the national press; and if it had not quite become "smart" to be a member, at least to confess your membership publicly was to evoke admiration." Admiration is the pressure this Tradition was built against, and it is far harder to stand than hostility ever was. Then came the case that tested the Tradition's own vocabulary. "A film star had gone so far as to break her anonymity on celluloid with the ﬁlming of her life story." Celluloid. Films — the third word in the Tradition, and the one nobody had expected to need. She broke it first in 1946 or 1947; the autobiography came in 1954; the picture in 1955. And then A.A.'s account of her adds a single short sentence and stops. "She subsequently drank again." No comment. No moral. No blame. The fact, set down where it can be read, and nothing built on top of it.

9eeba49bd89a.t: A.A.'s record of the most public break in its history adds one short sentence about what happened to her afterward, and then says nothing at all. What would I have added — and would it have helped anyone?

13b9b4e4fe5b.t: November 17 — "At All Hazards." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. In 1938 Frank Amos tr

228e4088abdb.t: In 1938 Frank Amos travelled to Akron for John D. Rockefeller, Jr. to find out whether this thing was worth money. His reports are the earliest written record of what A.A.'s founders were afraid of, and the fear is not the one you would guess. They were not afraid of being ignored. They told him (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers) "early publicity would be ruinous—because it would result in the few present workers' being swamped with requests from relatives and friends and from alcoholics themselves. As a consequence, the whole movement probably would bog down." Ruinous. Around forty people were sober across two cities, and the thing that frightened them was too many people wanting in. Amos recorded the other conviction the same year, and it is the sentence that has held for nearly ninety: "commercialization of this movement must at all hazards be avoided." At all hazards. Not where convenient, not where affordable. Both of those were written down eight years before there were any Traditions, and both survived into the wording of this one.

487a3b0f38f2.t: With forty people sober in two cities, what the founders feared most was too many people wanting in. What am I guarding so carefully that I have stopped asking whether anyone can reach it?

77fa52228418.t: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (Frank Amos's 1938 reports to Rockefeller).

c1c3c1390061.t: November 18 — "It Was Tottering and It Had to Fall." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films.

e2cc30e1f96d.t: It Was Tottering and It Had to Fall

995e6f5f8d52.t: There is a page in the Big Book (p. 385) where a man describes the summit of his career, and he does it with a list that ought to stop any A.A. member cold. "My professional life looked fine on the surface. I was now head of a publishing venture in which nearly a million dollars had been invested. My opinions were quoted in Time and Newsweek along with pictures. I addressed the public by radio and TV. It was a fantastic structure, built on a crumbling foundation. It was tottering and it had to fall." Read that list against the Tradition. Quoted, with pictures. Radio. TV. He is not describing an anonymity break — he was nowhere near sober and A.A. was nothing to him yet. He is describing what those things were doing for him, which was propping up a man who was already coming apart. That is why this Tradition names those media and not others. They are not dangerous because they are public. They are dangerous because of what being in them does to an alcoholic who is unwell, and his story is in the book so a member can recognise the feeling before he recognises the situation.

95b1108c6f02.t: He listed the press, the pictures, the radio and the television as the structure holding up a man who was already coming apart. What am I appearing in that is holding something up?

4c6357a52105.t: Grounded in: Big Book p. 385 ("Me an Alcoholic?").

514e614d7a8c.t: November 2 — "I Don't Want to Capitalize on Humility." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films

2f4b4e04c518.t: I Don't Want to Capitalize on Humility

ccb999c0555b.t: On 2 February 1954 Bill W. wrote to the Secretary of Yale University and turned down an honorary Doctor of Laws. He did not pretend it was cheap (Pass It On): "Were I to accept, the near term benefit to Alcoholics Anonymous and to legions who still suffer our malady would, no doubt, be worldwide and considerable." Yale had already solved the obvious problem for him — the citation would name him only as W. W. "True, the splendid citation you propose, which describes me as 'W. W.,' does protect my anonymity for the time being." He refused anyway, because a courtesy is not a record. "So, while I might accept the degree within the letter of A.A.'s Tradition as of today, I would surely be setting the stage for a violation of its spirit tomorrow. This would be, I am certain, a perilous precedent to set." He offered them an alternative: give the citation to A.A. itself, and "In such an event, I will gladly appear at any time to receive it on behalf of our Society." Then he asked the few who knew to say nothing about any of it — "I don't want to capitalize on humility."

51bdd8c1aafc.t: He refused an honour that would have helped A.A., and then made sure nobody heard he had refused it. What good thing have I done that I quietly arranged for the right people to find out about?

b1a0f6abe6b3.t: Grounded in: Pass It On (the Yale letter, February 2, 1954).

9c421ea9ee61.t: The Machine Only Carries the Ones Who Do

f0b62b1c5e13.t: This one has no villain in it, which is exactly what makes it hard to argue with. A platform has to decide what to show people. It measures what holds attention, and what holds attention is a face, a name, a day count, and a story told by someone who plainly means it. So it shows more of that. Recovery content made by people who identify themselves reaches thousands; the same content made anonymously reaches almost nobody. No outside body decided this. No meeting was captured. But the result is a mechanism that continuously selects for the exact conduct this Tradition asks members to avoid, and quietly buries the members who keep it. Given enough time that stops being a question about distribution and becomes one about doctrine, because the version of recovery the public can see is the version the machine promoted. And A.A.'s literature names a cost here that has nothing to do with the Fellowship's reputation (A.A. pamphlet P-43): personal anonymity breaks in the public media "not only may discourage timid prospects; they may threaten the anonymity-breaker's own sobriety." The machine cannot see that cost. It is paid, quietly, by the person the machine rewarded.

81acefffce13.t: The version of recovery most people can see is the one a machine chose to carry, and it carries the members who put their names on it. What have I come to think is normal purely because it was the part I could see?

4ae7c92391fc.t: An earlier break than the film star's, and a harder one, because Bill had said yes to it. Pass It On is direct about why: "Her case was a particularly sensitive one, because she was a close personal friend of Bill's. In addition, Bill strongly supported her work in alcoholism education." Marty M. was going out to tell the public that alcoholics are sick people and that something can be done for them — work Bill believed in and had encouraged — and she was formidable at it. "Marty made excellent newspaper copy as she toured the country." Bill's own account of how it started (A.A. pamphlet P-17) does not spare him. "A close A.A. friend of mine wanted to go in for alcohol education. A department of a great university interested in alcoholism wanted her to go out and tell the general public that alcoholics were sick people, and that plenty could be done about it. My friend was a crack public speaker and writer. Could she tell the general public that she was an A.A. member? Well, why not?" Well, why not. "I thought it an excellent idea and therefore gave my blessing." The uproar that followed was the Fellowship's. The permission had been his.

e7a85b402222.t: Bill encouraged the work, gave the permission, and then the Fellowship's anger landed on her rather than on him. When did I approve something and let somebody else carry what came of it?

178b14f1cc86.t: November 22 — "The Best Protective Gadget." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. A noted r

dd548579fcdd.t: A noted radio commentator broke his anonymity on the air and in the press, to an audience estimated at twelve million. Bill wrote about it to Jack Alexander — the <0>Saturday Evening Post</0> journalist, a friend of A.A. and not a member — and the letter is the clearest thing he ever put down about why this Tradition is not squeamishness (Pass It On). "Of course, this looks like wonderful publicity to folks outside A.A." Then the turn: "it is a danger signal." Not because the man was cynical. "He really thinks he is doing us a favor; he hasn't the slightest idea that he is busting the best protective gadget our Fellowship will ever have." A gadget. Bill did not reach for a spiritual word there, he reached for a mechanical one, because he was describing a device that does a job. Then he named the force it has to hold against, and noted that the force only grows: "As the value of the A.A. name for money raising and publicity purposes increases, so will the temptation." And finally why one man on the radio was worth a letter at all. "Most of us deeply realize that enough repetition of such blasts could alter the whole character of our Society."

ade9a543d5e7.t: Bill called anonymity a gadget — a device built to hold against a pressure that only ever increases. What in my life is doing a quiet mechanical job that I have mistaken for a nicety?

c123b00e77d8.t: Grounded in: Pass It On (Bill's letter to Jack Alexander).

5488577cc238.t: The part that gets forgotten is that a break is rarely one person's. A member who goes public goes public with a room behind him — the sponsor who gets named, the friend whose story is told because it makes the point better, the man whose relapse is useful as an illustration. The Big Book set the domestic version down in 1939 (p. 125), long before anybody imagined a camera in a pocket: "Another principle we observe carefully is that we do not relate intimate experiences of another person unless we are sure he would approve. We find it better, when possible, to stick to our own stories." Unless we are sure he would approve. That is already a high bar across a kitchen table. At the level of press, radio and films it is effectively unreachable, because the people whose stories travel along are not in the room when the decision is made, and they will find out the same way strangers do. A member can only ever consent for himself. The difficulty is that he is almost never only carrying himself.

6ef65f16a6e4.t: A member can only consent for himself, and he is almost never carrying only himself. Whose story have I told because it made my point better than my own would have?

b22bf2c3815d.t: The group has money — not much, eleven hundred dollars past the prudent reserve, gathered over four years of good Thursdays. Somebody points out, correctly, that there are people in this town who do not know A.A. exists. So they take a month on the bus shelter outside the hospital: the group's name, the meeting time, the address, one plain line about drinking. It costs six hundred and forty dollars. Two people come because of it and one of them stays, and that is not nothing — that is a life, and everyone involved was right about the need. Here is the difficulty, and it is not that advertising is wicked. The long form (Big Book, p. 565) says A.A. "ought to avoid sensational advertising," and a bus shelter is not sensational. But a group has just spent members' contributions to promote itself, publicly, under the A.A. name — a decision with no obvious stopping point that nobody in that room was authorised to take. Next year it will be two shelters. Because it worked.

8cd511772b18.t: A man came in off that bus shelter and stayed, and the group had spent members' money to promote itself under a name it was never authorised to spend. When has a thing working stopped me asking whether it was mine to do?

03cba6606471.t: November 25 — "Trained Doubters." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. Start with the debt

0c34be301c00.t: Start with the debt, because it is real and A.A. states it plainly (A.A. Comes of Age). "Without its legions of well-wishers, A.A. could never have grown as it has. Throughout the world favorable publicity has been the principal means of bringing alcoholics into our fellowship." Not one means among several — the principal one. And it is said without grudging: "Veteran newsmen, trained doubters that they are, have gone all out to carry A.A.'s message." So this mechanism has no villain in it either. A journalist wants to write something that will genuinely help. Her editor wants a named human being, because an unnamed one reads as unverifiable, and he is not wrong about that. The pressure lands on a member — not as a demand but as a favour, asked by somebody doing A.A. a kindness. Say no and the piece runs thinner, later, or not at all, and people who would have walked in won't. Say yes and the Tradition is gone in a single paragraph. There is no clever answer to this. There is only the fact that A.A. decided in advance, and in writing, which of those two costs it was going to pay.

2eed099b1b84.t: There is no clever answer to it; A.A. simply decided in advance which of the two costs it would pay. What have I left to be decided in the moment that would be far better settled now?

fbd93a9e6ab4.t: August 1939. "At this time, Dr. Bob wrote and may have signed an article on A.A. and the Big Book that appeared in the August 1939 issue of a magazine called Faith." May have signed. A.A.'s own history of its co-founder (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers) cannot establish whether his name was on it — and then it does something very few organisations would do. 4626a06000de.t: A.A. arrived at its public relations policy by first admitting, in print, what kind of people were writing it (A.A. Comes of Age). "By temperament many of us had been irresponsible promoters, and the prospect of a society composed largely of promoters was frightening." Frightening — about themselves. And Bill did not pretend the alternative was self-evidently wrong; he set the two side by side without any contempt for the other one. "A worthy charity wants to raise money, and so its letterhead shows the names of every distinguished person whose support can be obtained. Much of the political, economic, and religious life of the world is dependent upon publicized leadership. People who symbolize causes and ideas fill a deep human need. We of A.A. do not question that." Do not question it. It works, for other people, and he says so. "But we do have to face the fact that being in the public eye is hazardous, especially for us." So they took the other road — not because it was nobler, but because of who they were. "So we resorted to the idea that it would be far better to let our friends do this for us. And they have done it to an amazing extent."

3f92be8d4ec3.t: They wrote the policy by first admitting in print that they were, by temperament, promoters — and that a society of promoters frightened them. What do I know about my own temperament that I have never said out loud?

ffb09d177acb.t: He is ten years sober on the fourteenth, and the group's oldest member hands him the medallion at the Tuesday meeting. Afterwards, in the parking lot, he photographs it in his palm and posts it that night with four words about being grateful. It is a good post and he meant every word — and telling people he is sober, even that A.A. saved his life, one face at a time, is the most effective thing a member can do. But this is not one face at a time. It is two hundred, most of them strangers to that room. The photo is taken on the table by the door, the group's laminated meeting card lying beside it — name and night perfectly legible — and his own face in the reflection off the coin. In one post he has become what A.A. looks like for two hundred people, and he has taken the group along with him: its name, its night, its hall, and nobody in that room was asked. He carried it well, as it happens. That is luck. The Tradition asks that the Fellowship's face never be one man's face — however good the man.

3094862b66cd.t: November 3 — "Whether or Not the Name Is Given." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. A.A.

6125bae44a32.t: Whether or Not the Name Is Given

0206bd9206d3.t: A.A. answered the television question decades ago, and the answer is more exact than most members realise. From A.A.'s own literature (A.A. pamphlet P-43): "According to a Conference opinion, members are breaking their anonymity when they are identiﬁed on TV as A.A.'s and their faces are shown — whether or not their names are given." Whether or not their names are given. The face is the identification; the name was never the point. That sentence was written when television meant a studio, a crew, a broadcaster's permission and somebody else's decision. It now describes a phone held at arm's length by the person it protects. And notice that A.A. did not respond by refusing the medium. It went to real trouble to use it without supplying a face: "masks; screens; back-lighting that shows A.A.'s only as silhouettes; camera angles showing them only from the back." Elaborate, slightly ridiculous, and entirely deliberate. The reason is seven words long and it is the whole Tradition in miniature. "For we are not selling personalities — we are explaining A.A."

fe5ad93b513d.t: A.A. worked out that a face identifies a member as surely as a name, and then went to absurd lengths to appear on television without giving one. What do I show that says more than anything I actually said?

81f79bfc3764.t: Grounded in: P-43, The Twelve Traditions Illustrated (Tradition Eleven).

cdc68747fc04.t: November 30 — "People We Do Not Control." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. The Traditi

168451f492b4.t: The Tradition ends on a sentence that sounds like modesty and is in fact a supply chain (Big Book, p. 565). "There is never need to praise ourselves. We feel it better to let our friends recommend us." A.A.'s whole growth was built on that arrangement — doctors, clergy, judges, newspapermen and the man at the next desk, all recommending A.A. because they had watched it work and had nothing whatever to gain. Now hold the arrangement up and change one thing. The friend still recommends A.A. He is also being paid a referral fee, or he has beds to fill, or his platform earns on the click. Every word he says may be true. But the recommendation is no longer free, and a recommendation that is not free is an advertisement wearing a friend's face. A.A. cannot audit this, and has no standing to try. Which is why that closing sentence has to be read as the whole thing it is — not merely that we should stay quiet about ourselves, but that we depend, completely and permanently, on the honesty of people we do not control.

139a3b23f700.t: The entire arrangement rests on people who had nothing to gain saying so anyway. Who has spoken well of me when there was nothing in it for them — and have I ever told them it mattered?

9a6f588d5cef.t: November 4 — "Thirty-One People and a Cake." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. The grou

663cc29062cd.t: The group turns forty this month and somebody brings a camera. Thirty-one people, a sheet cake with the group's name piped across it in blue, the banner on the wall behind them. It is a good photograph. It goes up that evening with the group's name and the date, because that was the point of taking it. Twenty-nine of those people are perfectly happy. Two are not, and their reasons are nobody's business — that is the point. Whether a member appears in public as a member is a decision A.A. leaves to that member alone, every single time. The camera just made it for two people while they smiled, because saying no in a room full of friends costs more in the moment than it seems worth. The long form is specific about the medium (Big Book, p. 565): our names and pictures as A.A. members "ought not be broadcast, filmed, or publicly printed." Nobody in that hall broadcast anything. They took a nice picture at a party. The photograph is the broadcast — and it published a decision that was never the group's to make. Not because membership is a secret; because it is each member's own to tell.

afaff2a7a1f4.t: The photograph made a choice that belonged to each member alone, and two people smiled while it was made for them. Whose choice have I made by assuming they would be fine with it?

ab6b1895b8c1.t: November 5 — "The Face That Costs Nothing." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. A treatme

a76e660bbcd5.t: A treatment centre needs one thing it cannot manufacture: somebody credible saying it worked. Outcome figures are contested, the staff are paid, and everybody knows both. What settles a frightened family's doubt is a person who has been there, looking into a camera, telling the truth. So the facility asks a grateful former patient, and gratitude is real, and the answer is usually yes. Now look at what changed hands. That man's recovery very likely happened in church basements, for free, among people who never sent him a bill — and his credibility was built there. It is being spent here, in a market, on a business. A.A.'s own literature explains exactly why he is the one worth asking (A.A. pamphlet P-43): "Alcoholics who have recovered through our program are themselves the strongest attraction that A.A. has." He is the attraction. That is the asset. And when he mentions where he goes to meetings, an endorsement nobody voted on arrives attached to a name that has never endorsed anything, and there is nobody sitting on A.A.'s side of that table to say so.

b0a81ccfc0d5.t: His credibility was built for free among people who never billed him, and it got spent on a business that did. What did I earn in one place and spend somewhere else entirely?

318f6beb72b5.t: November 6 — "Bill the Broker." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. Bill W. told this sto

05621299b4ea.t: Bill W. told this story on himself for years. The ballplayer's break had worked spectacularly, and Bill's reaction was not caution (Pass It On). "Soon I was on the road, happily handing out personal interviews and pictures. To my delight, I found I could hit the front pages, just as he could. Besides, he couldn't hold his publicity pace, but I could hold mine." Read that again. He was competing. With a member, for column inches. "At the time, this looked like the thing to do. Feeling justified, I ate it up. What a bang it gave me when I read those two-column spreads about 'Bill the Broker,' full name and picture, the guy who was saving drunks by the thousands!" He called himself A.A.'s number one anonymity breaker. And here is the part that makes him worth trusting: it was not quite true. Lois's diary shows he barely left New York that year, and his real breaks came two years later. A.A.'s own biography says so — "But the truth is that he did not act on those feelings" — and explains why he told it worse than it was. He was "never afraid to use himself as a negative example (something he would not do to anyone else)."

abcbbbaeeea6.t: Bill accused himself in public of a break he had not quite committed, because he would use himself as the bad example and never anybody else. Whose example do I reach for when I want to make a point land?

b1b8b279898d.t: Grounded in: Pass It On (Bill's own account, and the book's correction of it).

e5bd2024cc9c.t: November 7 — "Two Ways to Break It." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. Most of what peo

ac21c9e6e9ec.t: Most of what people believe about this Tradition is one half of what Dr. Bob actually said. Warren C. recalled him laying it out complete (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers): "He [Dr. Bob] said there were two ways to break the anonymity Tradition: (1) by giving your name at the public level of press or radio; (2) by being so anonymous that you can't be reached by other drunks." Two ways. The second one is never quoted, and it is the one most groups are guilty of. Dr. Bob's own conduct followed the same line in both directions. He would not have his name in a newspaper — but when Akron members wanted to speak to Rotary and Kiwanis clubs in the 1940s, he approved it, and Joe P. remembered why: "he didn't think we would get anyplace if people didn't know we belonged to A.A. He had the firm conviction that you should let yourself be known as an A.A. member in the community, and he was always sure to tell you about it every time you met him." Every time you met him. He worried people would take the hiding half and stop there.

3e043d3fc42c.t: Dr. Bob said you break this Tradition by being unreachable just as surely as by being in the papers, and he repeated the second half every time he saw you. Which half have I been quietly comfortable with?

f56234dd94a1.t: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (Warren C. and Joe P. recalling Dr. Bob).

e33525b975c9.t: November 8 — "Too Quiet to Be Found." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. Here is the fai

a99582d4af1d.t: Here is the failure nobody feels guilty about. A group meets in a hall with no sign. Its listing has an old phone number that rings out. Nobody answers the email because nobody agreed to hold the account. The address circulates by word of mouth among people who already know it, and everyone involved believes they are protecting something. A.A.'s literature puts the cost plainly (A.A. pamphlet P-43): "Suppose a sick alcoholic never has the good fortune to meet an A.A. How is such a person going to ﬁnd us? The search will be difﬁcult if the local group thinks it should be anonymous, too." The group thinks it should be anonymous, too. That is the error stated exactly — personal anonymity read as institutional invisibility. The Tradition protects a member's name at the level of press, radio and films. It says nothing whatever about a meeting being hard to find, and a meeting nobody can find is not keeping a Tradition. It is just a room with the lights off.

2f134ce06b77.t: A meeting nobody can find is not protecting anyone's anonymity — it is only difficult to reach. Where have I called something discretion when it was mostly just easier?

999fb1c19821.t: November 9 — "The Recording Stayed Up." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. It was a hard

e87398422fe8.t: It was a hard winter and the group did a decent thing. Half the regulars couldn't get out, so somebody set up a camera at the back and streamed the meeting, and it worked — twelve people who would have sat at home alone were in the room instead. Nobody thought about the archive, because nobody was thinking about September in February. In March a man shared for eleven minutes about his brother, who had died in November, and about what he had said to him the last time they spoke. He was facing the camera. He did not know he was. What he consented to was a room: those faces, that night. The archive handed his story to an audience he never agreed to and cannot call it back from — in September his brother's widow finds it, because his brother's name is in it and she was searching for it. Everything about that group's decision was kind. But who hears a member's story is the member's own decision, made fresh each time he tells it — and a recording goes on making it for him long after the winter ends.

02307ad37a5d.t: A group did a kind thing for people who couldn't get out, and nobody was thinking about September in February. What am I doing right now that will still be findable long after the reason for it has passed?

ce244f6fee4a.t: October 10 — "A Silence That Large." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A.A.'s size gets used as testimony for positions nob

ab39b81c944a.t: A.A.'s size gets used as testimony for positions nobody in A.A. was ever asked about, and that is one more reason A.A. holds none. Someone arguing for a law, a funding model or a treatment contract reaches for the biggest number of sober alcoholics there is, and it appears in the submission as if those people agreed with the conclusion. Nobody asked them, and nobody has the standing to answer for them. The long form closes the door from A.A.'s side (Big Book, p. 565): "The Alcoholics Anonymous groups oppose no one. Concerning such matters they can express no views whatever." Bill W. gave the reason in 1955 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 4): "if we steadfastly decline all political, sectarian, or other alliances, we shall avoid internal division and public notoriety". An alliance means taking a side together with somebody else. Division is the danger to the drunk: a fellowship split over a law is a fellowship arguing instead of answering the phone. Today the borrowed number shows up whenever a program or a campaign says it speaks for millions in twelve-step recovery. Test it tonight: when someone tells you what people in recovery want, ask who asked them.

dd712def770e.t: No one can say what A.A.'s members want in an outside fight, because A.A. holds no view to report. When have I said what "people in recovery" think?

e273661abc01.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 10 (Big Book, p. 565); P-17, p. 4 (Bill W.'s foreword, 1955).

ca63524b74ff.t: October 11 — "The Other Side of the Same Fight." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. Both sides of the liquor fight wanted th

3b182ddd6824.t: The Other Side of the Same Fight

d75994d373f7.t: Both sides of the liquor fight wanted the same thing from A.A., its name on their side, and A.A. gave it to neither for the drunk's sake. Bill W. told how close it came (A.A. Comes of Age): a liquor trade association wanted to hire an A.A. member as an educator, to teach that alcoholics cannot drink at all, and to say in all its publicity that he was a member of Alcoholics Anonymous. Then the arithmetic: if the liquor trade got its educator, "the “drys” would instantly hire another A.A. member" to educate for their side. The drys were the people fighting to ban liquor. A.A. would have been on both sides of a fight it had no business in. Then the sentence this whole month stands on: "We simply could not take sides in this fight and do business with sick alcoholics too." Business, meaning the one job A.A. has: the man still drinking, who may work for the brewery or vote to close it. The member who was offered the job saw it himself: "Alcoholics Anonymous saved my life. It comes first." Today both sides of every alcohol-policy fight still claim the people in the rooms. Test it tonight: if someone at your meeting argues a drinking law, ask whether he is speaking as himself or for the room.

25f59d9e6b03.t: The wets and the drys wanted the same thing from A.A., and A.A. gave it to neither, because the drunk might be on either side. Which side of a fight about drinking does my room look like it's on?

a2d2d5aebc5a.t: October 12 — "A War Machine That Would Never Fight." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A weapon kept only for protection ge

060f41ad2de6.t: A War Machine That Would Never Fight

eb3616427487.t: A weapon kept only for protection gets used, so A.A. refused one that would have put it in public lawsuits. After a film studio nearly misused the A.A. name, the board's chairman proposed an act of Congress to protect it. The General Service Conference, the delegates the groups had sent, said no, and Bill W. recorded why (A.A. Comes of Age): "Under enough provocation, we would be bound to start public lawsuits and thus enter the field of public controversy. It would be like building a war machine on the theory that it would always stay home and never fight." A fellowship in court is a fellowship on one side of a public fight, and the papers print the side. The committee's resolution named the cost: A.A. could become tangled in lawsuits without end, and the expense and the publicity could threaten its very existence. So the Conference chose to "rely upon group and public opinion for our ultimate protection." Picture the drinker who reads that A.A. is suing somebody. He does not learn that A.A. is free; he learns that it fights. Today the war machine is a lawyer's letter sent in A.A.'s name. Test it tonight: ask whether anyone near you has threatened legal action for A.A., and who gave them the right.

98ce35cebcbf.t: A.A. turned down the power to sue because a fellowship in court has taken a side in public. Has anyone threatened a fight in my group's name?

39f34efcee25.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (Tradition Ten: the Congressional Charter; the Conference resolution).

d9330dca2528.t: October 13 — "Known." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A member known to be in A.A. who takes a public side can implicate

5ab68f6767a5.t: A member known to be in A.A. who takes a public side can implicate A.A. without once saying its name. The long form is exact about when a member's opinion becomes A.A.'s problem (Big Book, p. 565): only when it is expressed "in such a way as to implicate A.A." That is the whole of it; his own vote, faith and views are his. But implicating A.A. does not need the word. A man everyone in town knows got sober in those rooms, standing at a microphone for one side of a drinking law, is heard as the rooms speaking, whatever he says about himself. The Big Book's first Foreword told the public what A.A. is (p. xiv): "We are not allied with any particular faith, sect or denomination, nor do we oppose anyone. We simply wish to be helpful to those who are afflicted." Nor do we oppose anyone. A known member at a podium can make that sentence look false to the one person it was written for: the drinker on the other side, who concludes the rooms are against him. Today it is the professional recovery voice, introduced at hearings and on panels by how long he has been sober. Test it tonight: when someone is introduced by his sobriety before he argues a cause, ask what the audience will hear.

9cf8b55d52e4.t: A member can implicate A.A. without naming it, just by being known and taking a side. When I take a side in public, what do people who know I'm sober hear?

da21b142c194.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 10 (Big Book, p. 565); Big Book p. xiv (Foreword to the First Edition).

30158ce07435.t: October 14 — "However Good." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A group cannot sign its name to any other cause, however goo

b5f71037f3e7.t: A group cannot sign its name to any other cause, however good, and Bill W. wrote the good case into the refusal on purpose. The letter is true: a detox is closing, a program for drunk drivers is losing its money, and other organizations have signed. A member asks for the group's name too. Nobody wants the group's opinion; they want its standing. Bill W. answered in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 24): "we can say quite emphatically that neither A.A. as a whole nor any A.A. group ought to enter any activity other than straight A.A. As groups, we cannot endorse, finance or form an alliance with any other cause, however good". However good. He knew every real request would be a good one; a line that bent for good causes would bend for all of them. Straight A.A. means the message carried to the drinker, and nothing else. The long form gives the reason (Big Book, p. 565): "The Alcoholics Anonymous groups oppose no one." A group that signs for one side of a funding fight has opposed the other, and some drinker is on the other side. Today it arrives as a sign-on letter or a coalition list. Test it tonight: ask whether your group's name is on any letter, list or coalition, and who put it there.

440b0dde4269.t: Bill wrote "however good" into the refusal because every request that reaches a group is a good one. Has my group's name gone on anything that isn't straight A.A.?

639c5f366a4c.t: Grounded in: P-17, p. 24 (Bill W., 1947); long form, Tradition 10 (Big Book, p. 565).

90c56cf53a0c.t: October 15 — "A New Instrument for Social Action." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A.A. was praised as a new instrument f

675d83a06bc8.t: A New Instrument for Social Action

4cf27882bdaf.t: A.A. was praised as a new instrument for social action and never took the job, and that refusal is why its good spread. The Lasker Award citation of 1951 sits in the back of the Big Book (p. 571): historians might one day see A.A. as "a great venture in social pioneering which forged a new instrument for social action". An instrument for social action is a tool for changing society, which is the job description of a reform movement. It was meant as praise. A.A. printed it and kept doing one thing. Bill W. told what that restraint bought (A.A. Comes of Age): "We saw that the more A.A. minded its own business the greater its general influence would become." Medicine, religion and psychiatry began to borrow its ideas, while A.A. lent its name to no cause but its own. Minding its own business is what keeps the door open to the drunk: a man who needs A.A. tonight does not have to agree with anyone's plans for society to walk in. Today the capture comes as praise: programs and campaigns that describe A.A. as a platform for their cause, a partner in their mission. Test it tonight: when someone describes A.A. as part of something bigger, ask what the bigger thing wants from it.

Comes of Age): "Sometime in 1940 a temperance worker at Toronto showed the A.A. book to an alcoholic who had resisted all other attempts at rescue." 8a021e43db70.t: A.A. stays out of every public fight, even the good ones, because recovery is life itself to the drunk and a fellowship in a fight can die. Bill W. said (A.A. Comes of Age) that A.A. had known from the beginning that "no matter what the provocation," it "must never publicly take sides" — "in any fight, even a worthy one." Provocation means something that tempts you to hit back. Even a worthy one: he wrote the hard case into the principle, not beside it. Then the reason: "we do not enter into public controversy, because we know that our fellowship will perish if we do." Perish means die. And the sentence that says whose life is at stake: "Recovery from alcoholism is life itself to us, and we wish to preserve in full strength our means of survival." The means of survival is the rooms, open to any drunk. A worthy fight still has two sides, and the man still drinking may be on the other one. Today the worthy fight arrives with a death toll and a deadline, and someone says this one is different. Test it tonight: when someone says the rooms should speak up on something, ask whether the drinker on the other side would still walk in.

c1efa83f0533.t: Bill wrote "even a worthy one" into the principle because the worthy fights are the ones that pull. Is there a cause I want my room to speak up for?

b5ff71ae3e34.t: A candidate at the podium in campaign season tells every voter on the other side that this room is not his. The invitation was innocent: he is a good speaker with long sobriety, and this year he is also running for office, and the flyer carries his name. The Big Book describes who fills A.A.'s rooms (p. 17): "many political, economic, social, and religious backgrounds. We are people who normally would not mix." People who normally would not mix. That only works in a room that has no side. The A.A. Preamble, printed at the front of pamphlet P-17, says what A.A. is: "not allied with any sect, denomination, politics, organization or institution; does not wish to engage in any controversy; neither endorses nor opposes any causes." A newcomer comes that night who knows the speaker's name from the lawn signs on his street. He watches a room full of alcoholics applaud the man he voted against. Nobody endorsed anyone; the flyer and the applause did it. Today it is the speaker night or anniversary that doubles as a campaign stop, or the local official invited to say a few words. Test it tonight: look at who has been invited to speak at your meeting this year, and ask what else their name stands for right now.

185964076d70.t: October 2 — "As We Elect." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. Dr. Bob's last major talk said A.A. would grow or die by what

79a157e03ec1.t: Dr. Bob's last major talk said A.A. would grow or die by what it refused to get mixed up in. Detroit, 1948 (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers): "It is possible for us to grow or not to grow, as we elect." Then his conditions: "If we fight shy of entangling alliances, if we avoid getting messed up with controversial issues (religious or political or wet-dry), if we maintain unity through our central offices, if we preserve the simplicity of our program, if we remember that our job is to get sober and to stay sober and to help our less fortunate brother do the same thing, then we shall continue to grow and thrive and prosper." Wet-dry was the fight over whether liquor should be legal. Religious, political, wet-dry: the same three fights the long form of Tradition 10 names (Big Book, p. 565). And the list ends on the drunk, the less fortunate brother still drinking. The refusals come first because they protect that job. Today it is quieter: an "A.A. meeting" printed on a program's schedule beside the program's public positions on drug policy or funding. Nobody at the meeting says a word, and the meeting is allied anyway. Test it tonight: whose name besides the group's is on your meeting's door or schedule, and what is that name on record for?

04eea5bd823f.t: Dr. Bob put the fights A.A. refuses ahead of everything else, and ended on the drunk those refusals protect. Is my meeting tied to anyone who has taken a side?

48964c4c8b06.t: Money from either side of a fight comes with the side attached, and A.A. named that danger early. ba456760e0cb.t: Nobody speaks for A.A. in a fight, and that includes the man who started it. 6902fa817239.t: Tradition 10 asks the most of the people who love a fight, which is most of us, and it asks for one reason: the drunk. Bill W. did not pretend otherwise (A.A. Comes of Age): "Considering how most of us have really loved controversy, this denial of the privilege of attacking something or somebody in public is no small achievement for the naturally aggressive people that we are." Controversy means a public argument. Naturally aggressive: he meant us. Giving up the right to go after someone in public is a real sacrifice, and Bill wrote it down as one. We have but one purpose: to carry the A.A. message to the sick alcoholic who wants it." Rip society asunder means tear it apart. The sick alcoholic who wants the message might be on either side of any of those three fights. Today the fight comes into the room through the shares: the news of the week, a politician's name, a sneer at somebody's church. Test it tonight: listen for anything said in your meeting that a newcomer from the other side would take as a door closing.

A name on a supporters' list is a side, and the man still drinking who is on the other one can read that list too. Today it is the sponsor board at a fundraiser, the logo wall at a recovery walk, the community partners page. Test it tonight: search your group's name online and see what list it is on.

3771caa8f48d.t: In the Name of A.A. and Our Group

6f9ddaa26a30.t: A member who protests a law in A.A.'s name speaks for people who never agreed, and the drunk who disagrees hears that A.A. is not for him. The pamphlet P-43 draws Tradition Ten as a cartoon. A member stands up to thank A.A. for ten sober years, and then: "But before I leave" — he is "sending a telegraph in the name of A.A. and our group" to protest a bill before Congress. A telegraph here means a telegram, the fastest message of the day. His next line: "I know I speak for all of A.A." Out in the room, someone on the other side of that bill says what the whole Tradition is afraid of: "How could anyone get sober or stay sober in an outfit like that?" That is the drinker P-43 wants you to see. He came for a way out and found a political club. The long form says the groups "oppose no one" (Big Book, p. 565), and the cartoon's member opposed someone on everybody's behalf. Nothing about his ten years was false. His telegram was. Today it is the petition, the open letter or the rally sign sent from the recovery community, with A.A. meant to be read into it. Test it tonight: when anything is sent in your group's name, ask who in the room agreed to it.

4e88c8844af9.t: Two members assumed A.A. was angry on their behalf, and the newspapers told the country it was. Bill W. told it (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 55): "A member, whose name and professional attainments are known on three continents, got hold of a letter which she thought damaged her professional reputation. 1115217ad1d1.t: October 27 — "Into Public Controversy." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A.A.'s own parent movement was dragged into a pub

c8a5f39de0a6.t: A.A.'s own parent movement was dragged into a public fight, and Bill W. would not even thank it in public, because the drunk's chance came first. The Oxford Group, the Christian movement where Bill and Dr. Bob first found help, made the newspapers in 1936 when its leader was quoted praising a dictator; Pass It On records that "the article brought the group into public controversy." In 1940 Bill wrote to a member who asked about it (Pass It On): "unfortunately, a vast and sometimes unreasoning prejudice exists all over this country against the O.G." O.G. means the Oxford Group. He was grateful; some of its message, he wrote, had saved his life. But thanking it in public might "establish a connection between the O.G. and Alcoholics Anonymous which does not exist". So: "I had to ask myself which was the more important" — his own pleasure in paying the debt, "or that alcoholics everywhere have the best possible chance to stay alive regardless of who gets credit." A drinker who hated that fight would have taken A.A. for part of it. Today the pull is gratitude too: a church, a program or a funder that helped the group and wants its name beside A.A.'s. Test it tonight: ask whose name your meeting wears besides A.A.'s, and what fight that name is in.

d58c9501f94f.t: The Big Book set out to give no one a reason to argue about medicine or religion, so nobody can use A.A. to settle those fights for you. Its writers knew (Big Book, p. 19): "Of necessity there will have to be discussion of matters medical, psychiatric, social, and religious. We are aware that these matters are, from their very nature, controversial. Nothing would please us so much as to write a book which would contain no basis for contention or argument." Psychiatric means about mental illness; contention means a fight. On health, the same book sends the reader outward, to the people whose work it is (p. 133): "Do not hesitate to take your health problems to such persons." A.A. holds no view on your prescription, your diagnosis or your church for anyone to quote. The long form adds sectarian religion to the fights the groups stay out of (p. 565). The drinker this protects is the one on a medication, or of a faith, who gets told at the door that A.A. is against it and goes back out. Today it is staff, or a member, telling a newcomer what A.A. believes about his pills. Test it tonight: if someone tells a newcomer what A.A. thinks about his medication or his church, ask them for the page.

45e66e6fcd7a.t: October 29 — "Our Sole Aim." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. Saying plainly what A.A. is has never been an outside issue;

13067ca0d435.t: Saying plainly what A.A. is has never been an outside issue; it is the one thing A.A. must say. Tradition 10 keeps A.A. out of other people's fights, not out of its own name. Bill W. drew the line in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 24): "we cannot link the A.A. name to other enterprises in the alcohol field to the extent that the public gets the impression we have abandoned our sole aim." Sole aim means only purpose. An enterprise is a business or a program. The pamphlet P-43 says it in a caption: "Ours is not a secret society" — "we carry the message anywhere we can". Saying out loud that an A.A. group charges nothing and answers to no program is not taking A.A. into a fight. It keeps A.A.'s name its own. The drinker who thinks A.A. is a program he can't afford, or a place he'll be reported from, never finds the free room down the street. Today the confusion sits on intake forms, billing sheets and websites that list twelve-step meetings as a paid service, which an A.A. group never is. Test it tonight: ask whether your meeting answers to anyone but the alcoholics in it, and say so out loud when someone asks.

33e99fedf2f5.t: Tradition 10 keeps A.A. out of other people's fights; it never asks A.A. to let others say what it is. Could a drinker tell, from what my room says about itself, that it is free and answers to no one?

71c971628943.t: October 3 — "No Views Whatever." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. Read Tradition 10 in its long form before anyone tells y

0e80e0dbc7c9.t: Read Tradition 10 in its long form before anyone tells you what it means, because the words are narrower and harder than the rumour. The Big Book (p. 565): "No A.A. group or member should ever, in such a way as to implicate A.A., express any opinion on outside controversial issues—particularly those of politics, alcohol reform, or sectarian religion. The Alcoholics Anonymous groups oppose no one. Concerning such matters they can express no views whatever." Whose views? The groups', and a member's only when it drags A.A. in with him. Which fights? Outside ones: elections, liquor laws, one church against another ("sectarian" means belonging to one denomination). What it does not say is that A.A. must keep quiet about itself. What an A.A. group is (free, run by its members, answering to no one) is A.A.'s own business, not an outside issue. The reason for the silence is the drunk: a man still drinking who hears the rooms are against his party or his faith has a reason not to come. Today the words get turned around. Staff tell a client "A.A. says" something about his medication, his church or his vote. Test it tonight: when anyone says "A.A. says," ask to see where it is written.

cd25bb089b8e.t: Tradition 10 closes A.A.'s mouth on outside fights, not on what A.A. is. Have I ever repeated "A.A. says" about something A.A. has never said?
