395a096d3d13.t: October 30 — "Practically Never." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. Tradition 10 is kept first inside the room: a group tha

97ea794a2031.t: Tradition 10 is kept first inside the room: a group that never argues these fights in private will never argue them in public. Bill W. passed on what one old-timer told him (A.A. Comes of Age): "Practically never have I heard a heated religious, political, or reform argument among A.A. members. So long as we don't argue these matters privately, it's a cinch we never shall argue them publicly." A cinch means a sure thing. Akron remembered the same habit from the early 1940s; Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers sums up how Joe P. recalled the local thinking: "If you had something wrong with you, that's what you talked about; you didn't talk about sports or politics." That is not a gag. It is a room with one subject: the drinking, and the way out. And it is why Bill could say that "Our fellowship never has taken sides publicly on any question in this embattled world" — a world full of fighting. A newcomer from any side of any fight could sit down in those rooms and hear nothing that told him to leave. Today the news walks in with every phone, and the shares drift toward it. Test it tonight: count how many minutes of your meeting are about drinking and recovery, and how many are about everything else.

d106aba530fa.t: The rooms that keep this Tradition are the ones where the fights never come up, so no drinker has to hear which side the room is on. What does my meeting spend its minutes on?

0688200a34d4.t: October 31 — "We Were That Excited." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. The month ends with A.A. nearly breaking this Tradit

65763e833d5c.t: The month ends with A.A. nearly breaking this Tradition over its own name, and Bill admitting why. A film studio wrote a script about A.A.; Bill W. judged it (A.A. Comes of Age): "The proposed portrayal of A.A. seemed pretty lopsided and in rather bad taste." A portrayal is how a film shows something. "We concluded that we ought to ask for an injunction against the company for misuse of the A.A. name." An injunction is a court order to stop, so this meant going to court. It worked. Then Bill wrote the line that belongs at the end of this month: "Otherwise, we might have sued, forgetting all about A.A.'s principle of non-controversy in public." Then: "We were that excited." The people who wrote Tradition 10 nearly broke it defending A.A. itself, because defending something you love feels like it can't be wrong. A lawsuit would have put A.A. in the headlines as a fighter, and the drinker reading them would have learned the rooms had enemies. Saying what A.A. is costs nothing; going to war for it costs the drunk. Today the excitement comes the same way: someone misuses A.A.'s name, and the room wants a fight. Test it tonight: the next time you feel sure A.A. needs defending in public, ask what the drunk still out there would read about it.

98df7d66079b.t: The people who wrote Tradition 10 nearly broke it over A.A.'s own name, because they were that excited. What am I excited enough about to forget it?

754d1fd75714.t: October 4 — "Eleven to Two." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A group that votes on an outside issue now has an opinion on

6dc42b1e08db.t: A group that votes on an outside issue now has an opinion on it, and a drinker on the losing side has just been shown the door. It happens at the end of a business meeting, after the coffee money. Someone brings a petition about a local liquor law. There is no argument; the room agrees. A show of hands, just so we know where we stand. Eleven up, two down, and the secretary writes it in the minutes. No newspaper, no statement. But the group has a recorded position, and the long form's line is crossed: "in such a way as to implicate A.A." (Big Book, p. 565). Bill W. described what groups that last do instead (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 38): "The groups are willing to avoid controversy over outside issues such as political reform or religion; they stick to their single purpose of helping alcoholics to recover." Single purpose. The two who kept their hands down may stay or may drift, and the drinker who hears about that vote from them may never come at all. Today the request usually comes from outside: a campaign asking groups to "sign on." Test it tonight: ask what your group's business meeting has ever voted on, and whether every item was A.A.'s own business.

bd7a648c00d4.t: A show of hands turns an outside opinion into a group's position, and some drinker is always on the other side of it. Has my group ever voted on something that wasn't A.A.'s business?

8fc7337ad5f7.t: October 5 — "Evangelist or Reformer." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. Before there were any Traditions, the Big Book's in

f1b6e2a91487.t: Before there were any Traditions, the Big Book's instructions for carrying the message already ruled out the crusade, because a crusade costs you the drunk. Chapter 7, Working With Others (Big Book, p. 89): "Don't start out as an evangelist or reformer. Unfortunately a lot of prejudice exists. You will be handicapped if you arouse it." Six pages later, sitting with the man still drinking (p. 95): "You will be most successful with alcoholics if you do not exhibit any passion for crusade or reform." A reformer, like a crusade, is out to change how everybody else lives; an evangelist is selling a faith. Either one makes the sick man pick a side before he can pick up the phone. Tradition 10 is the same instruction written for a whole group: what would handicap one member at a bedside handicaps a room in front of a town. Today the crusade comes in through a door marked "A.A. meeting" at a facility, where the program's cause is read before anyone shares: its doctrine, its position on the latest law. Test it tonight: could a drinker from either side of any argument sit down in your room and not be told what to think?

e1f5502ea477.t: The Big Book told the first A.A.s not to come to a drunk as reformers, because prejudice shuts the door. Is anything said in my room that would shut it?

b71dfb847742.t: The first member who dragged A.A. into a public fight was sure he was helping, and that is what made him dangerous. Bill W. (A.A. pamphlet P-17, pp. 52–53): "Presently an A.A. member began to publish a crusading magazine devoted to the cause of Prohibition. He thought Alcoholics Anonymous ought to help make the world bone-dry." Prohibition was the law that banned liquor outright. He told his readers he was an A.A. member. "He pointed out that he too was an “educator,” and that his brand of education was the “right kind.” As for putting A.A. into public controversy, he thought that was exactly where we should be." Now read it as the man still drinking. He picks up a magazine that says A.A. wants his bottle outlawed. He does not hear one member's opinion. He hears that the rooms are a temperance society, and he does not call. The long form names this exact fight, "alcohol reform" (Big Book, p. 565), because it is the one a drunk is surest to be on the other side of. Today the "right kind of education" comes printed in a program's brochures and campaigns about drinking, with A.A. named as if it had signed on. Test it tonight: find where your meeting is advertised, and read what else that page says.

be83269c2745.t: A sincere member put A.A.'s name on a Prohibition magazine, and every drinker who read it learned the rooms wanted his bottle. What does my room's name say to a man who is still drinking?

1d9e354a9c73.t: Radio lectures that were half A.A. and half one man's religion would have told a whole country that A.A. was his church. A member had been paid to give twelve talks about A.A. on national radio, and headquarters read the scripts first. Bill W. (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 53): "They were about 50% A.A. and 50% our friend's personal religious convictions. This could create a false public view of us. Religious prejudice against A.A. would be aroused. So we objected." Think about who would have been listening. A drinker of another faith, or of none, hears that A.A. is one man's creed, and the door he needed closes before he reaches it. The Big Book had already drawn the line for a member sitting with one drunk (p. 94): "We are dealing only with general principles common to most denominations." The long form draws it for the whole Fellowship: no opinion on "sectarian religion," meaning the teaching of any one church (p. 565). A.A. stopped the broadcast without a word in public, and the man dropped it. Today the same half-and-half turns up in a meeting run as somebody's ministry, where the host's doctrine is read from the front as if it were A.A.'s. Test it tonight: is anything read at your meeting that belongs to one faith and not to A.A.?

427ce039353b.t: A group account cannot post as one member; every word it sends out is the group's. The long form's line is not about intentions (Big Book, p. 565). It is "in such a way as to implicate A.A.," and an account with the group's name on it implicates the group every time it speaks. Bill W. saw what one member could do once he made the A.A. name his to use (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 53): "it was in the power of an A.A. to marry Alcoholics Anonymous to practically any enterprise or controversy at all, good or bad." Marry, meaning tie together for good in the public's mind. He was describing a man who had to declare his membership to the whole public to do it. Today it takes a password. A meeting starts a page so people can find the schedule, and one night the news touches drinking, or an election, and whoever holds the login shares something. It reads as the group's view, because there is nothing else it could read as. And somewhere a man still drinking, scrolling for a meeting at midnight, finds out which side the room is on before he finds out what time it starts. Test it tonight: ask who holds your group's password, and read back everything that account has posted that isn't about meetings.

f6945bdfb38b.t: September 1 — "Not an Organization." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Akron, 1937. Eighteen alcoholics sat in a li

1db14edc90be.t: Akron, 1937. Eighteen alcoholics sat in a living room while Bill W. made his case: A.A. should hire paid missionaries, build a chain of hospitals that turned a profit, and publish a book. The room pushed back hard. Then it voted, and Bill won — "by the barest majority, and over the most strenuous objections," in his own account of it (A.A. Comes of Age). A.A. had just decided, democratically and in good faith, to turn itself into an organization. Nobody in that room was cynical about it. They believed structure would reach dying men faster, and they may well have been right. It never happened. Bill went east to raise the money and came back with nothing. Two years later the Big Book went to print, and page xiii carried the first thing A.A. ever said about itself in public: "We are not an organization in the conventional sense of the word." That sentence survived because a fundraising trip failed. It's also why the meeting you sat in this week has no owner, no dues, no membership committee, and nobody with the standing to put you out.

7571dc31c4d2.t: September 10 — "The Missing Clause." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. The whole safeguard in Tradition 9 is six wo

662132bfc07e.t: The whole safeguard in Tradition 9 is six words, and they are the six that get left out. The short form (Big Book, p. 562): "A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve." Service boards and committees are the offices that answer the phone, print the schedules and keep the lights on. Quote the Tradition without the ending and you have a permission slip — A.A. allows offices. Quote it whole and you have a leash: any body doing A.A.'s work answers downward, to the people it serves, or it is not doing A.A.'s work. That is the cheapest capture there is. Nobody has to lie. A sentence stops early, gets repeated, and starts to sound complete. So when a board, an office, a committee, or a program tells you it is part of A.A., ask the six-word question: who do you answer to? An A.A. service body answers to the groups, and the groups can stop paying for it tomorrow. A body that answers to owners, funders, or a head office is organized in exactly the way this Tradition says A.A. never will be. Read the Tradition to the end. The end is the point.

ff04ed07a86c.t: The safeguard is six words most people stop before. What have I accepted as settled because I only heard the first half?

b022ec394be0.t: September 11 — "Let Him Stay." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Nobody stands at the door of an A.A. meeting decid

483fc9080ec5.t: Nobody stands at the door of an A.A. meeting deciding who gets in. That was settled by the drunks who tried it. Early Cleveland had men posted for exactly that job — other members called them the "snifters," which an early member explained were "men who stood by the door, sniffing each man who came in" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers). Sniffing for liquor. Behind them stood the rules: you had to be hospitalized first, or visited by ten members, or passed by a committee. Then a man walked in with a couple of drinks in him. The snifters moved to throw him out, and somebody said: "Let him stay. Maybe something will seep in." He stayed. He got sober, "just as sober as the fellow who had been hospitalized or visited by ten members, there went another rule. In the end, pioneer A.A.'s broke so many of their own rules that there were no rules left!" That is where the open door came from. So when a programme puts an assessment, an intake, or a sign-off between you and a chair, understand what it is: the snifters, back at the door. The alcoholic still drinking is the whole reason the room exists. A.A. learned not to make him qualify for it.

fff44821c437.t: A.A. broke its own rules until none were left, because the drunk at the door was the point. Would I have got in the night I came?

0f4c6ecb3936.t: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers.

c9127e7a88a9.t: September 12 — "Nobody Runs It for Life." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Nobody runs an A.A. group for life. The

907b0bbbbb01.t: Nobody runs an A.A. group for life. The Long Form says how it is done in one short sentence (Big Book, p. 565): "Rotating leadership is the best." The drunks in Cleveland worked that out before anyone wrote it down. In October 1939 they formed A.A.'s first central committee — seven people — and built the exit into it from day one: "one man and one woman dropped off each month to be replaced by the next in line according to seniority" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers) — seniority meaning time in A.A., not rank. Bill W. admitted what everyone had assumed until then: "Up to that time, all of our affairs had been in charge of the ultra-oldtimers, and we naturally supposed it would always be that way." Naturally supposed. That is how a person becomes a position — not by a vote, but by nobody thinking to ask. Rotation is the ask, built in, so the job always comes open and never turns into a man. It is also why the chair will be open to you. Now look at any room where the same person has run "the A.A. meeting" for years and is paid to. Nobody is rotating out of a salary. That room has a manager, and A.A. groups do not.

2aa1502147a2.t: A.A. built the exit into its first committee so no job could become a person. When did the chair in my meeting last change hands?

85f4444a2bf2.t: Grounded in: Big Book, long form, Tradition 9 (p. 565); Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers.

9a3337c39feb.t: September 13 — "We'll Get Around to You in a Minute." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. The moment a group owns a t

b128b27ac3ab.t: We'll Get Around to You in a Minute

7f00fc5ffeac.t: The moment a group owns a treatment operation, the newcomer becomes the least urgent thing in the room. A.A. has the case on record (P-43, The Twelve Traditions Illustrated): in the early days some members thought "A.A. should cover the whole alcoholism field," and one group "built an all-purpose center, including a section for drying-out treatment" — a building of its own, with beds. The pamphlet asks you to picture it: "Arguments over cost, architecture, staff, fees, medication, and rules might even make the local paper." And pity the poor newcomer straying into the group — "We'll get around to you in a minute." Cost, staff, fees, rules — every one of those is a thing somebody has to govern, and Tradition 5 says a group has one purpose, carrying the message to the alcoholic who still suffers. The centre failed. The lesson did not. The same page gives the standing practice: "keep the operation of the facility completely separate from that of any A.A. group," and keep the A.A. name, and terms like Twelfth Step, out of the facility's name. Read that against today's storefronts. A business with "12 Step" on the sign and beds down the hall is the all-purpose centre, rebuilt. The newcomer is still being told to wait a minute.

e84e3a90e7f6.t: A.A. tried owning treatment once and the newcomer got told to wait. Where am I being made to wait behind somebody's fees?

cbf1e55c4029.t: Grounded in: P-43, The Twelve Traditions Illustrated (Tradition Six); Big Book, long form, Tradition 5 (p. 563).

c11898062176.t: September 14 — "Couldn't Be Organized." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. The heart of A.A. cannot be organized, an

a301c0e1ee76.t: The heart of A.A. cannot be organized, and anyone offering to organize it is selling something else. A.A.'s own pamphlet says what "A.A., as such" means in Tradition 9 (P-43, The Twelve Traditions Illustrated): it "goes to the heart of the A.A. experience" — one alcoholic saying, silently perhaps, "Help!" and another answering, "I know how you feel. We're here to help you." Then the verdict: "Such a relationship couldn't be organized." Then it shows what trying looks like — a desk, a questionnaire, a computer matching you to the right helper — and the newcomer walking out the door. That is the whole of it. A.A. does organize the coffee, the phone and the rent, and the pamphlet is exact about how far that goes: "those who take part in A.A. service work are assuming responsibility — not taking on authority." Responsibility for the coffee. No authority over you. And one line to carry into any building: "Tradition Five applies to each A.A. committee and board as directly as it does to each A.A. group." Every body in A.A. exists to carry the message, and only that. A body that assesses you, schedules you and bills for the hour has organized the one thing A.A. said could not be.

6ee2ee9c473b.t: One drunk says help, another answers — that cannot be organized, and the pamphlet says so. Has anyone tried to organize that for me, and what did it cost?

e0b4e56ed95f.t: Grounded in: P-43, The Twelve Traditions Illustrated (Tradition Nine).

c36bccc52125.t: September 15 — "Responsibility, Not Authority." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Every service job in A.A. looks l

51fa1ebec731.t: Every service job in A.A. looks like a position, and none of them are one. The pamphlet is exact about the difference (A.A. pamphlet P-43): "All the way from coffee-brewers to trustees on the General Service Board, those who take part in A.A. service work are assuming responsibility — not taking on authority." Then it lists who answers to whom, and the list runs one way only. "Group officers are responsible to the members of the group; intergroup committees, to the groups in one locality," and on up until "the General Service Office and Board and the board's committees, to all groups and members everywhere." Hold that against the way every other organisation you have dealt with is built. The same pamphlet does it for you: "In an average business corporation, the board has final power to determine company plans and policy." And then A.A.'s: "In industry, branch offices jump when the home office speaks. Our GSO is just a clearinghouse of A.A. information, offering suggestions based on experiences reported to it by groups." So the question to ask about anything doing A.A.'s work is not what it is called, or who runs it, or whether they mean well. It is which way the sentences run. A body that reports to the people it serves is doing A.A. service. A body that instructs them has become something else, and it did not need to announce the change.

3a585e4cb697.t: Every job in A.A. is a responsibility somebody accepted, never an authority somebody was handed. Who does the person running my meeting answer to, and how would I find out?

3dd4182c06b4.t: September 16 — "The Screening Committee." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. No committee decides who is fit for A.A

0be118c16721.t: No committee decides who is fit for A.A. Oscar W. helped start a group, went back to visit, and found four ministers in the front row (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers). He was delighted — four ministers in A.A.! One of them stood up and set him straight: "We're not drunken ministers, We are the screening committee for Alcoholics Anonymous, to determine who is fit for membership." Read the title again. Not friends of the group. A screening committee, ruling on fitness, in a fellowship whose only requirement is a desire to stop drinking. Nobody invaded that room. Somebody invited them, because they were respectable and seemed like the right people to have around. That is how it happens — not by force, by help. The Long Form leaves no gap for it (Big Book, p. 563): "we may refuse none who wish to recover." None. Not by a minister, a clinician, or an intake form. So when a building tells you it will "assess" whether you are ready for A.A., you are looking at four ministers in a front row. A.A. has no screening committee. It never accepted one.

a48c8f781bd2.t: Somebody invited the ministers in because they seemed like the right people. Who have I let decide whether I qualify?

696dc0a1b593.t: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers; Big Book, long form, Tradition 3 (p. 563).

30e64a02186d.t: September 17 — "A Legal Bludgeon." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. A.A. was offered the power to govern, by law,

636e57354ddb.t: A.A. was offered the power to govern, by law, and turned it down. After a film studio misused the A.A. name, the board's own chairman — a lawyer — proposed a Congressional Charter, an act of Congress protecting the name the way the Red Cross is protected. Bill W. was honest about what headquarters saw in it (A.A. Comes of Age): "a legal bludgeon of this size and weight could easily be used" on anyone who still defied the law. "It looked like a grand idea and we at the Headquarters were all for it." The delegates — the members the groups had sent — said no. Their reasoning is the plainest sentence in this month: "It would mean the legal organization of a fellowship whose Traditions insisted on its being unorganized." Their written finding went further: "A Congressional incorporation would create by law a power to govern which would be contrary to, and violative of, our Traditions." A power to govern. That is what A.A. refused, even to protect its own name from people misusing it. So hold that against anyone today who wants to hold the name, license the meetings, or certify who may carry the message "to protect A.A." A.A. already decided what protection costs. It chose the open door and no bludgeon.

045b39420bf6.t: A.A. refused a law protecting its own name because the protection came with a power to govern. What protection have I wanted that would have cost more than the thing it protected?

2e229fc77b15.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (the Congressional Charter; the Conference resolution).

24a34778dbd5.t: September 18 — "Still Around." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. The people this Tradition guards against are not h

44185026441b.t: The people this Tradition guards against are not history. A.A.'s own pamphlet says so in the present tense (P-43, The Twelve Traditions Illustrated): "And they're still around — the members who are always sure that they're always right — the members who are happily ready to assume all the burdens of leadership and grimly unwilling to share them, let alone give them up." Read the two halves. Happily ready to take it on. Grimly unwilling to hand it back. Usually the same person, usually someone with real sobriety who has done real good — which is why nobody catches it early. There is no villain, only a grip that tightened so slowly the group adjusted around it. The pamphlet's next line is the answer, and it is not "find that person": "But a group does need officers. How can we cope with this dilemma?" The Traditions cope by building the group so it does not matter when that person shows up — jobs rotate, nobody governs, and the newest drunk in the room owes nobody at the front a thing. Now put a salary under that grip, and a job title, and a building. The grimly-unwilling member is still around. Today he can be on payroll.

c4469d618e8f.t: The people to watch for take the work on happily and hand it back grimly. Am I holding anything happily that I would hand back grimly?

91f92309b4d1.t: Grounded in: P-43, The Twelve Traditions Illustrated (Tradition Two).

374018e5b195.t: September 19 — "The Expanded Program." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. A group can only be about one thing, and t

606676783087.t: A group can only be about one thing, and the moment it is about two, the newcomer has to guess which one he came for. A.A. has the case (P-43, The Twelve Traditions Illustrated): one group offered an "expanded A.A. program" — one "that included helping newcomers to find jobs." Good people, real help, real results. The pamphlet's finding is exact about what breaks: "when the group turns itself into an employment agency, newcomers may get confused about their primary purpose. A.A.'s function is to help them get sober — then they can find work for themselves." Confused about their purpose — the newcomer's, not the group's. And the pamphlet draws the line around the whole category: "the A.A. group as a whole is not a friendly finance company, nor a welfare department, nor a housing bureau." Now read a treatment brochure. Housing, employment support, life skills, family programming, and "A.A. meetings" — bundled, scheduled, and invoiced. That is the expanded program, at scale, with the one thing A.A. exists for listed as an amenity. The Tradition does not say the other help is worthless. It says a room that is about everything cannot be unmistakably about the drunk who just walked in.

0edc0c2199b9.t: Helping with jobs was good, and it left the newest man guessing what the room was for. What have I added to something good until the point of it got hard to find?

30d6cbd07ec1.t: September 2 — "Won't Money Spoil This Thing?." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. December 1937. Bill sat in John D.

f700f7d134a8.t: December 1937. Bill sat in John D. Rockefeller Jr.'s board room and asked for money to build something specific: a chain of hospitals where alcoholics would be treated, staffed by A.A. members, paid for out of the proceeds. Albert Scott, who chaired the trustees of Riverside Church, asked the question that ended it (A.A. Comes of Age): "Won't money spoil this thing?" Rockefeller sent a man to Akron to look, got back a recommendation for fifty thousand dollars, read it, and said no. "I think money will spoil this." Be clear about what A.A. almost became. Not a fellowship that referred people to hospitals — a fellowship that owned them. Beds, staff, fees, admissions, discharges. And whoever owns the building has to govern it: decide who gets in, who pays, and who is asked to leave. That is an organization, and Tradition 9 is the sentence saying A.A. can never be one. Tradition 9 asks one thing of any body doing A.A.'s work: is it "directly responsible to those they serve" (Big Book, p. 562)? Nine years after that board room, A.A. wrote the answer down, so it would never again depend on a rich man saying no.

88d1c8f96a43.t: Rockefeller's refusal is the only reason A.A. didn't end up owning the places where people get sober — that was luck, not principle, and it held exactly once. Where in my own recovery am I still counting on luck to hold again?

bc95ff5e69e7.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (the board room; Rockefeller's refusal); P-44.

d3a319fc8eaf.t: September 20 — "The Absence of a Boss Is Not a Vacancy." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Here is the move that us

9dedf930bb13.t: The Absence of a Boss Is Not a Vacancy

92e0160ce99e.t: Here is the move that uses Tradition 9 against itself: read "ought never be organized" as a confession that A.A. is amateur and unmanaged, then offer to supply the management. Bill W. answered it before anyone made the offer (P-44, A.A.'s Legacy of Service, p. 3). A.A. has services — meeting places, offices, phones, literature, committees, trustees — and "Nor can we make A.A. more simple by abolishing such services. We would only be asking for complication and confusion." A.A. is not unstructured. It refuses one kind of structure: the kind that governs. And Bill gave the only test A.A. applies to its own machinery: "Concerning any given service, we therefore pose but one question:" — "Is this service really needed?" — and the answer carries a duty: "If it is, then maintain it we must, or fail in our mission to those who need and seek A.A." Read who that test is for. Those who need and seek A.A. — the alcoholic still out there. Not owners, not funders, not a head office. That is a question the Fellowship asks about itself, and it is not an opening for anyone else to answer on its behalf. When a programme says it will organize A.A. for its clients, the absence of a boss is not a vacancy. It is the design.

c118d39368da.t: A.A. refuses one kind of structure on purpose, and the empty chair at the top is not waiting to be filled. Where have I mistaken somebody's restraint for a job opening?

9aaed478c610.t: Grounded in: P-44, A.A.'s Legacy of Service (p. 3).

ead34df00c9e.t: September 21 — "A Great Many Sheets of Paper." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Every rule was reasonable. Added t

b4d8ab2359d7.t: A Great Many Sheets of Paper

4137c998b716.t: Every rule was reasonable. Added together they would have kept nine out of ten of A.A.'s own founders out. Around 1943 the head office asked every group to send in its membership rules. Listing them, Bill recalled, "took a great many sheets of paper" (Pass It On). Then he did the arithmetic: "If all these edicts had been in force everywhere at once, it would have been practically impossible for any alcoholic to have ever joined A.A. About nine-tenths of our oldest and best members could never have got by!" Nine-tenths. Including the men who wrote the rules. No group had done anything cruel. Each had added one requirement, for one good reason, after one bad night — and no one could see the total until somebody stacked the sheets. That survey is the closest thing A.A. has to a photograph of what organizing a fellowship does to the person it exists for. Today the sheets have new names: intake criteria, readiness assessment, programme eligibility, discharge conditions. Each one sensible. Stack them and ask the only question that matters: could the drunk who needs this room tonight get by them? A.A. asked that once, and threw the sheets away.

e38acfef0ecc.t: A hundred sensible rules would have kept nine-tenths of the oldtimers out. What have I built from reasonable decisions that I have never once looked at all together?

75536edd04ed.t: Grounded in: Pass It On (the membership-rules survey).

eca391e03968.t: September 22 — "Servants of Your Group." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. The committee that runs A.A.'s business

3ef27f7b6e57.t: The committee that runs A.A.'s business is made of servants, and the co-founder sat in the second row to prove it. Dan K. sat on Akron's Central Committee — "the steering committee for the office" — and remembered a night the words flew "like you were in a barroom" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers). Dr. Bob stood up, put up his hands, and said: "Gentlemen, please. We're still members of Alcoholics Anonymous. Let's carry the principles of A.A. into these business meetings. You are servants of your group, here to take the ideas formulated by the committee." Read the order. First what they are — members, the same as anyone in the room — then what they are for. Servants. Not managers. Joe P. remembered the same man at meetings: "He'd go to a meeting, and he wouldn't sit up on the stage. He'd always sit in the second row or someplace like that." That is the whole Tradition, lived before it was written, by a man who never held a title in A.A. and never needed one. So look at where the people running today's rooms sit, and what they hold. A clipboard at the front is not a chair in the second row.

d466fade1616.t: Dr. Bob ran nothing, sat in the second row, and stopped a brawl by reminding servants they were servants. Where do I sit when I think I am in charge?

5ba7e02299ba.t: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (Dan K. and Joe P.).

bd87bd7df1c4.t: September 23 — "Now Dr. Bob Said." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. A.A. has nobody who can give orders, so people

4ead87fc1c8d.t: A.A. has nobody who can give orders, so people manufacture authority the only way left — by borrowing it from the dead. Joe P., who knew Dr. Bob, watched it start while the man was barely gone (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers): "others are always repeating things Dr. Bob said that I know he didn't." And he named why: people say "Now Dr. Bob said …" in order to lend a little importance to what they are saying. That is the mechanism, from a witness. Mostly it is not lying. It is a person who wants to win a point, knows their own name will not carry it, and reaches for one that will. Today the borrowed name is often not a founder's. It is "the program." The program requires this. The program says you must. Tradition 9 took titles away from the living; quoting authority that does not exist is how a title gets smuggled back in. The defence is dull and it works: ask where it is written. Everything the founders actually said is on paper, the paper is in your hands, and it has never needed anyone to speak for it.

52f7e1b14bd0.t: With no one to give orders, people borrow authority from the dead or from "the program." When someone tells me what A.A. requires, have I asked where it is written?

ec99f1b70d0c.t: September 24 — "Bleeding Deacons." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Every group gets one, and A.A. gave him an unk

df78a8c753d5.t: Every group gets one, and A.A. gave him an unkind name on purpose. Bill W. traced what happens to a founder after his group votes in a rotating committee (A.A. Comes of Age). Some become elder statesmen, willing "to sit quietly on the side lines patiently awaiting developments." The other kind — the bleeding deacon — is "one who remains convinced that the group cannot get along without him, who constantly connives for re-election to office, and who continues to be consumed with self-pity." He is not lying about the work. It is a lot of work and nobody thanks him, and he says so, and saying so is how a job stops being one anybody else feels able to take. Then Bill does the thing that makes this survivable: "Nearly every old-timer in our society has gone through this process in some degree. I have myself." Not a warning about someone else — about anyone who serves long enough. A.A. built the cure into the structure: he can be voted out. Now picture him with a job title and a salary in a building that holds "the meeting." No election reaches that man. The deacon is still bleeding; today he cannot be rotated out.

7ffe4a971206.t: The bleeding deacon is convinced the group cannot get along without him, and Bill said he had been one. Where have I made myself necessary and called it helping?

617b97b9ccd3.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (elder statesmen and bleeding deacons).

2dd22fb86a63.t: September 25 — "The Name, Incorporated." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Whoever owns the name can license it, wi

c708dd889fe7.t: Whoever owns the name can license it, withhold it, and set conditions on it — which is why nobody in A.A. is allowed to own it. A.A. learned this in court, from its own members. The Service Manual records "a pretty hard-bitten lawsuit wherein two factions of AA's were competing for the possession of the A.A. name for Intergroup use, the name having been incorporated by one of them." Members. Both sides. In court over a name the Tradition says belongs to no one — and the fight was only possible because one side had filed paperwork to hold it, probably to protect it. That is capture in its purest form: not an outsider, an insider converting a shared thing into a held thing. The day after the filing, every alcoholic in that city needed permission for something that had been theirs by right the day before. Now look at recovery businesses with a registered name and "12 Step" or "Anonymous" in it. A registered name has an owner; an owner has a lawyer; a lawyer can decide who may use the words. A.A. does not license meetings. Nobody holds a right to the rooms, and nothing you need tonight is behind anyone's trademark.

599d3cff8c36.t: Two groups of members went to court over a name nobody owns, because one side filed paperwork to protect it. What did I take ownership of to protect — and did protecting it stay the point?

719ab8888ac6.t: Grounded in: A.A. Service Manual, Concept XII (Warranty Five).

33774169fa1a.t: September 26 — "Officials." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. A.A. got its first officials by accident, from a sign

b1ce32f0a8f0.t: A.A. got its first officials by accident, from a signature on a lease. New York's early members wanted a home, so they took over a former artists' club on West 24th Street (P-17, p. 19). "A couple of older members signed the lease. We painted and we scrubbed. We had a home." Then the headaches Bill lists on the next page: dictators ran amuck, steering committees "tried to nominate their friends to succeed them" and found, to their dismay, that even sober drunks couldn't be steered. And the sentence that is the whole problem (p. 20): "A corporation was formed to take over the clubroom lease so we then had" — Bill's own quotation marks here — officials. "Should these" directors "run the club or would it be the A.A. rotating committee?" Two authorities where there had been one, and nobody had intended a second. They only needed a signature. The lesson A.A. drew was not never sign anything. It was: hold property and business apart from the group, by people who answer for the property, so a group never has to ask which of its two authorities is the real one. Today's version needs no lease. A facility owns the room, the schedule, and the chair, and calls what happens in it A.A. That is directors running the club. The Tradition already answered which authority wins: neither. A group is not run.

0ae4f65aba98.t: A lease needed a signature and A.A. woke up with officials. Who owns the room I sit in, and do they think they own the meeting?

46e56bc1f8c6.t: Grounded in: P-17, A.A. Tradition: How It Developed (pp. 19–20).

0c7367f3f2cb.t: September 27 — "Safe, Even From Me." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. When A.A. finally built the structure that w

fdf06f367b09.t: When A.A. finally built the structure that would outlast its founders, the founders wrote it so the structure could overrule them. Bill W. sat on the board. He wrote the Conference charter so the groups' delegates could give that board orders. Then the first Conference met, in 1951, and did exactly that (P-44, A.A.'s Legacy of Service, p. 19): the delegates took up questions headquarters was unsure of, "sometimes giving advice contrary to our own conclusions. In nearly every instance, we saw that they were right." The groups had overruled the office, and the office had been wrong. They went further and renamed the Alcoholic Foundation, because the word Foundation "stood for charity, paternalism and maybe big money. A.A. would have none of these." Then the line to carry out of this month: "As I watched all this grow, I became entirely sure that Alcoholics Anonymous was at last safe — even from me." The man who could have kept it wrote the document that took it from him, and said he was relieved. Measure every recovery body you meet against that. Who can overrule its founder, its owner, its director? If the answer is nobody, it is not safe from anyone.

f4af83e1d398.t: Bill wrote the charter so the delegates could overrule him, and said it made A.A. safe from him. What would I have to give up for the thing I care about to be safe from me?

e1f73593da76.t: Grounded in: P-44, A.A.'s Legacy of Service (p. 19).

a510e6ba46f8.t: September 28 — "Never Organized At All." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Tradition 9 got stricter, on purpose, af

23740463c33a.t: Tradition 9 got stricter, on purpose, after fifteen years of practice. The first version was mild. Bill W. quoted it himself at St. Louis in 1955 (A.A. Comes of Age): "When Tradition Nine was first written it said," — "Alcoholics Anonymous needs the least possible organization." A matter of degree — keep it light. Then: "In the years since then, we have changed our minds about that. Today we are able to say with assurance that Alcoholics Anonymous—A.A. as a whole—should never be organized at all." And he said what the words mean, so nobody could soften them: "What we really mean, of course, is that A.A. can never have an organized direction or government." No direction. No government. Read what happened there. A fellowship reviewed a principle, watched what organizing did to the people it was for, and voluntarily cut its own power to govern itself — with no scandal forcing it. Anyone who tells you the Traditions are old letters nobody revisits should be handed this one. A.A. revisited it and tightened the rope on itself. So a body that directs your recovery, on a schedule, under a director, and calls itself A.A. is claiming the one thing A.A. said with assurance it would never be.

5a1c96f4024b.t: A.A. reviewed this Tradition after fifteen years and chose a stricter line, with nothing forcing it. When did I last review something I believe and come out holding a tighter line?

5904533e6d71.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (St. Louis, 1955 — Tradition Nine).

be21297da7d0.t: September 29 — "Servants, Not Senators." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. An A.A. committee cannot judge you, advi

7289d5ffdb39.t: An A.A. committee cannot judge you, advise you, or order you, and it can be voted out at the next election if it tries. Bill W. described what a group is left with once it has thrown off its founder and elected a rotating committee (A.A. Comes of Age): a body "very sharply limited in its authority. In no sense whatever can its members govern or direct the group." Then the exact limits: "It can give no spiritual advice, judge no one's conduct, issue no orders." And any committee member "may be promptly eliminated at the next election if he tries to throw his weight around. The members fully realize that they are actually servants, not senators." Three things a committee cannot do, and one thing the group can always do to it. That is the entire relationship between anyone at the front of an A.A. room and anyone in the chairs. So run the test on the meeting in the building. Does the person running it give spiritual advice you are expected to take? Judge your conduct — attendance, attitude, progress? Issue orders? And the fourth: can the people in the chairs vote that person out? A committee that fails the first three has become senators. A room that cannot do the fourth has been governed. Neither is an A.A. group, whatever the sign says.

cf9aa6665905.t: No spiritual advice, no judging conduct, no orders — and the group can remove anyone who tries. Could the people in my meeting vote out the person running it?

8660f78caa6d.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (the rotating committee's limits).

5f95e877be51.t: September 3 — "In the Supposed Interest of Efficiency." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Rotation looks like a bug

cd2c59c64286.t: In the Supposed Interest of Efficiency

3d8bab2f334a.t: Rotation looks like a bug. Start there, because pretending otherwise turns this Tradition into superstition. Your group finds a treasurer who is genuinely good — books balanced, rent paid early, nobody has to think about it. Six months later he rotates off and the new one is slower. Multiply that across secretary, G.S.R., literature and coffee, and the group spends a real part of every year worse at its own business than it was last month. Every argument for keeping the good one is correct. Bill saw that argument coming and named the word it would arrive under (A.A. Service Manual): "In the future — at those times when the rotation system does not work perfectly — there will be the natural demand to throw it out in the supposed interest of efficiency." He doesn't deny the inefficiency. He grants it and refuses the trade anyway, because rotation was never buying competence. It buys this: no job in A.A. quietly becomes a person, and nobody has to be talked out of a role he's held long enough to call his own. It's also why the chair is open to you in two years.

3f4d719efd04.t: A.A. accepted a worse-run office in exchange for a seat that always comes open. What am I holding onto because I'm better at it than whoever comes next?

34aa61e0ef02.t: Grounded in: A.A. Service Manual, Concept XI; long form, Tradition 9.

c3b41317b4aa.t: September 30 — "Read It to the End." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Tradition 9 only makes full sense when you r

784fed556c27.t: Tradition 9 only makes full sense when you read it to the end, past the short form and into the Long Form (Big Book, p. 565): "true leaders in A.A. are but trusted and experienced servants of the whole. They derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern." Servants of the whole means they work for the members, not the other way round. No title in A.A. lets anyone run you. The short form everyone quotes points the same way in its last words (p. 562): service boards or committees "directly responsible to those they serve." Today the Tradition gets cut short in rooms that call themselves A.A. but answer to someone else: a facility that books the meeting, pays the person at the front, and can cancel it. The person at the front of that room has a title and a boss, and neither one is the members. That room was organized, just not by the people in the chairs. Test your room tonight with three questions. Who could close it? Who does the person at the front answer to? Can anyone here put me out? In an A.A. group the answers are the members, the members, and nobody. That is the room the drunk still out there needs to find open.

48521c98be25.t: The Long Form says A.A.'s leaders are servants who do not govern. Who does the person at the front of my room answer to?

3490163724c9.t: September 4 — "The Man Who Started It." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. He is right about most things. That's the

27e5c0c8f55b.t: He is right about most things. That's the problem. A group starts because one man rented the room, bought the urn, and chaired the first eleven meetings when nobody else could. Five years on there are forty people, a rotating committee on paper, and not one decision he doesn't shape. Nobody appointed him. Nobody would object — he's the reason a good number of them are sober. Bill described this drift without softening it (A.A. Comes of Age): at the start, "these first members are his hierarchy, literally." Then comes the reasoning, and it never sounds like ambition. It sounds like care. "After all, we are experienced. Besides, look at all the good we have done those drunks. They should be grateful." The group hasn't been taken over. It's been looked after so well it never learned to stand up. And the cost lands on the newest person there. Disagreeing isn't disagreeing with a position — it's disagreeing with the man who saved him, and he knows it before he opens his mouth. So he says nothing, and the room gets quieter, and the quiet gets called unity.

dc6659d6b755.t: Nobody voted that man in, which is exactly why nobody can vote him out. Whose approval do I check for before I say what I actually think in a room?

9cc1788654c0.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (the local founder and his hierarchy); long form, Tradition 9.

5ed6126ce28e.t: September 5 — "Which Way the Money Runs." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Tradition 9 says two things, and the fa

0a700e73538f.t: Tradition 9 says two things, and the famous half is the wrong one. First: A.A. ought never be organized. Then the exception — it may create service boards or committees, the offices answering the phone. That's the permission; the safeguard is the condition riding on it (Big Book, p. 562): those bodies stay "directly responsible to those they serve." Bill explained how that clause gets enforced (A.A. pamphlet P-17): money, not anyone's character. "If any of them were to become inefficient or overbearing the remedy is simple enough. The average A.A. would stop his financial support until conditions were changed." Follow it around: the people served are the people paying, so they can stop paying, so the body serving them can't afford to stop serving them. That's a circuit, not a virtue. Responsibility runs whichever way the funding runs — automatically, whether anyone intends it or not. Now apply that to any body doing recovery work that's paid for by clients, insurers, or owners. It can be staffed by decent people. It can run a good program. It still answers upward, because that's the only direction the circuit allows. No villain required. So when you're working out whether something is A.A. or something wearing A.A.'s clothes, don't ask what it says about itself. Ask who could close it by keeping their money in their pocket.

cd60669df06f.t: The people who could shut down my home group are the people sitting in it. Is that true of everything else I lean on to stay sober?

1683215ca687.t: Grounded in: P-17 (stop his financial support; serve us well or go out of business); short and long form, Tradition 9.

ff817af25bde.t: September 6 — "Rule-Making Benders." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. A frightened group makes rules, and the rule

7353b8be21c4.t: A frightened group makes rules, and the rules do more damage than the thing it was frightened of. Bill W. watched it happen to nearly every early group and named it in A.A.'s own pamphlet on the Traditions (P-17, p. 13): "At one time or another most A.A. groups go on rule-making benders." A bender is a binge. The group grows fast, a few members drink, a few hit the room up for money, and the steady ones get scared for the thing they love. So they vote: "Charters, bylaws and membership rules are excitedly passed and authority is granted committees to filter out undesirables and discipline the evildoers." Now the room has a committee with the power to put a drunk out. That is what Tradition 9 means by organized. Bill recorded the result one page later (p. 14): enforcing the rules caused more trouble "than the very worst that the worst ever did." The rules were dropped. The people they were written to keep out stayed, and the group came to regard them "not as menaces, but rather as our teachers." No A.A. group needs a committee to protect it from its own newcomers. It never did.

4a90f9e7f6c7.t: The rules hurt the group more than the drunks did, so A.A. threw out the rules and kept the drunks. Who has decided I need protecting from — and what has that cost?

53c676c1f221.t: Grounded in: P-17, A.A. Tradition: How It Developed (pp. 13–14).

85d07acbcdd7.t: September 7 — "Shouted Down." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Nobody governs A.A. — not even the man who started

623fecb85c26.t: Nobody governs A.A. — not even the man who started it. Bill W. tried. He was the co-founder and the author of the book, and the groups refused him every time. He wrote it down himself (P-17, p. 40): "Each time I have strenuously tried it I have been shouted down." And: "After struggling a few years to run the A.A. movement I had to give it up — it simply didn't work." The groups put it plainly (A.A. Comes of Age): "We are not going to have a personal government in New York, or anywhere else. Services, yes. But government, no." Hold on to that when someone in a room, or a building, tells you how A.A. is going to be run. If the groups would not take orders from Bill W., they are not taking orders from a program director, a counsellor, or the oldest member at the table. Tradition 9 is not an idea somebody had. It is the record of what happened to the one man best placed to govern A.A. He lost, wrote the loss down, and made it permanent.

569407433f6d.t: The groups refused to be governed by the man who founded them. Who have I let govern my recovery who has less claim than he did?

a73c4c8630da.t: Grounded in: P-17 (p. 40); A.A. Comes of Age.

a94d781d804b.t: September 8 — "No Real Authority." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. In A.A., a title carries no power. None. The L

24f8f6b16af6.t: In A.A., a title carries no power. None. The Long Form of Tradition 9 (Big Book, p. 565) says it in one line: "true leaders in A.A. are but trusted and experienced servants of the whole. They derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern." Secretary, chair, treasurer, trustee — each is a job somebody took on so the coffee gets made, the rent gets paid and the office stays open, and each one rotates. Nobody holds a rank. Nobody can tell you what to do. The Big Book states the founding decision the same way (p. xix): "our leaders might serve but never govern." So look hard at the titles that come with today's meetings. Facilitator. Coordinator. Program director. Clinical lead. Those are real jobs in the buildings that pay for them, and inside an A.A. group they mean nothing. If the person at the front of the room has authority over you — can require you to attend, can remove you, can sign off on your progress — that room is being governed, and A.A. groups are not governed. Whatever it is, it is not the thing this Tradition describes.

3e8979f9bcca.t: No title in A.A. carries authority; everyone at the front is a servant who rotates out. Whose title have I mistaken for the right to run me?

1a08c71f322b.t: Grounded in: Big Book, long form, Tradition 9 (p. 565); Foreword to the Second Edition (p. xix).

4a93efd336c9.t: September 9 — "Well Outside A.A.." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. A meeting a facility can cancel is a meeting t

7a4ac019382e.t: A meeting a facility can cancel is a meeting that facility governs, and an A.A. group is governed by nobody. The Long Form is exact about where treatment belongs (Big Book, p. 564): "hospitals, as well as other places of recuperation, ought to be well outside A.A.—and medically supervised." Places of recuperation — where people go to dry out — outside. Not partnered, not hosting, not in-house. The same page closes the door on the arrangement itself: "An A.A. group can bind itself to no one." And Tradition 3 sets the one condition on being a group at all — two or three alcoholics may call themselves an A.A. group "provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation" (p. 563). Now look at the meeting on a treatment schedule. The facility picks the time, picks the room, staffs the chair, fills the seats with its clients, and can strike it from the calendar. That meeting is affiliated — tied to the facility — bound, and governed. Call it the facility's meeting. It is not an A.A. group, and nobody who runs it can tell you what A.A. requires of you, because A.A. requires nothing. The real thing is a room where the people in the chairs are the only ones who can close it.

55a28b0cac9e.t: Whoever can cancel the meeting governs it. Who can cancel mine?
